articles.title: How UW’s solar vehicle team harnessed the sun and hard work to shine on the national stage
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: In a cramped corner workspace in a mechanical engineering building at the University of Washington, a team of students is working to harness the power of the sun.

They operate on a fraction of the budget of elite international programs, fitting build hours around class schedules and other extracurriculars. Yet this summer, the scrappy crew took their handmade, solar-powered car — dubbed Sakura — out of the shop and onto the open road.

Over seven days in July and 1,778 miles from Minnesota to Texas, they outpaced nearly every competitor to finish fourth overall and cross the line as the top-ranking American team in the American Solar Challenge .

Now entering its fourth year, the Solar Vehicle Team at UW (SVTUW) is still a relative newcomer to collegiate solar racing. Officially affiliated with the university’s Mechanical Engineering Department, the roughly 50-person group has evolved into a broader interdisciplinary effort spanning electrical engineering, computer science, business, aerodynamics, and more.
Operated entirely by undergrads, the club handles every aspect of the operation in-house — from sponsor outreach and logistics to hands-on fabrication .

While top international competitors rely on multi-million dollar budgets and years of development , the Huskies assembled their vehicle (named after the Japanese word for cherry blossom) in just 11 months — a lightning-fast turnaround for a machine built entirely from scratch .
For team president Rudy Heredia-Jantz , an electrical and computer engineering senior, even making it to the starting line felt like a triumph.

“Frankly, we have no idea [how we pulled it off],” Heredia-Jantz said. “This car — it was a little bit of a miracle. We did not have it up and running until the day before we left for competition. We didn’t even have it moving. We just spun the rear motor, threw it in the trailer, and figured we’ll blow something up eventually.”

Things did indeed blow up — 12 tires in total along the way — but the Huskies kept rolling . For a third-year program competing against seasoned international juggernauts, simply keeping the car on the road was an achievement; outpacing them was a statement .
UW didn’t just survive the route to Texas — they blew past expectations for a young club, clinching the Aesthetics Award and Spirit of the Event Award alongside their top-four finish.
For second-year mechanical engineering student Elijah Yan , who serves as the team’s mechanical lead, the learning curve was immediate.
“Building a car is just not something I’ve done before, so it’s very new to me, and it’s super cool to learn that type of stuff — suspension stuff, how to do vehicle dynamics,” Yan said.

That hands-on engineering paid off when Sakura hit highway speeds on open pavement. Designed to maximize efficiency, the ultra-lightweight vehicle — weighing roughly 500 pounds with a driver inside — stretches 19 feet long to fit its array of solar panels while keeping its profile as narrow as possible.
Under the hood, Sakura is a blend of precision engineering and strict energy conservation :

To pull off a competitive build on a shoestring budget, the team combined its resourcefulness with local industry support. The vehicle’s lightweight frame, for instance, relies on carbon fiber sandwich panel flooring donated by Boeing, held together with specialized fiberglass tape.
“It’s the perks of being a Seattle-based team — we work with some amazing materials,” Heredia-Jantz said .
Yet even with aerospace-grade composites, bringing a prototype car across the finish line required plenty of improvised shop hustle.
“The car is held together with cardboard and duct tape, essentially,” Yan joked.
And managing the technical hardware on the road is as much a game of data processing as it is driving.

During the race, a dedicated strategy team monitors Sakura ‘s health in real time. Using a custom dashboard that feeds off the onboard smartphone’s data stream, students track battery state-of-charge, individual array voltages, and motor temperatures from a trailing support vehicle.

By pairing live telemetry with incoming weather forecasts, the crew calculates optimal cruise speeds on the fly — relaying instructions to the driver via walkie-talkie so they can balance energy consumption, leverage regenerative braking, and avoid tripping the battery’s protection systems on steep climbs or hard accelerations.

That real-time power management was also put to the test right before the cross-country journey, when the team competed in the Formula Sun Grand Prix — an annual three-day track race where cars run on a single initial charge and whatever sunlight they can harvest along the way. Despite navigating a track that pushed their power distribution system to its limits, the track time gave the team crucial baseline data and momentum before taking on the road race.

Now the club is already preparing for its next evolution. While repairing Sakura for upcoming competitions, students are designing their next-generation vehicle from scratch — overhauling power distribution, reinforcing the chassis, and building a new solar array.
For a club building sun-powered technology in a city known for grey skies, the project is ultimately driven by something deeper than weather .

“I believe this team is building something special in the early morning hours on UW’s campus: talent that shows up before sunrise, a refusal to wait for better resources before doing great work, and a stubbornness that looks a lot like faith,” said Caoilin Krathaus , the team’s administrative lead. “It reminds me of the story behind Boys in the Boat , and what I’ve always thought of as the true Husky experience.”

articles.title: UW, Microsoft and E8 back climate tech incubator targeting data centers as AI energy concerns surge
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: As public concern grows about the environmental impact of AI data centers, the University of Washington is launching a startup incubator to support climate tech innovations addressing those challenges.

UW CoMotion Labs is partnering with Microsoft and the investment network E8 to create a four-month program targeting technologies in areas including backup energy storage, grid improvements, efficient data center cooling, electronics waste reduction and low-carbon building materials.

“This is a really important initiative,” said Karin Kidder, executive director of E8. “The other really great part about this is it’s elevating the Pacific Northwest. There’s so much good work happening here.”

CoMotion has previously run two climate tech incubator cohorts, the second of which wrapped up Tuesday with a public demo event. The new effort is the first to focus on a specific industry within the climate space. Organizers are seeking early-stage applicants with technologies ready to commercialize, deploy as pilot projects or scale.

“Meeting growing demand for digital infrastructure requires continued innovation across energy, water, materials, and cooling,” said Brandon Middaugh, Microsoft’s general manager for sustainable markets, in a statement.

E8, which has invested $77 million in climate startups over two decades, will provide an investor-in-residence to advise founders and a representative on the startup selection committee. Microsoft will share technical and industry expertise and other support. Both organizations are providing funding for the effort, but the UW did not say how much.

In addition, the climate tech investment group Elemental Impact previously launched a Data Center Innovation Initiative to similarly address these challenges and will offer advisory support for the Seattle-based program.

The kickoff for the CoMotion Labs initiative coincides with a poll released Wednesday finding that 53% of Americans are “extremely or very concerned” about the environmental impacts of AI, up from 41% a year ago.

The survey, from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago, found that 80% of adults are concerned about data center effects on electric bills, power outages or water supply. The computing facilities are a central issue in the upcoming elections.

When it comes to technologies to lessen the burden of data centers, “these solutions are needed today,” Kidder said. “So I’m hopeful that while some of these solutions may be a couple years out, some may be relevant for today.”
Sarah O’Sell, manager of CoMotion Labs’ climate tech incubators, said one strategy will be connecting startups with partners and customers to speed deployment of new technologies.

“We recognize that climate solutions aren’t necessarily always looking for venture investment,” she said. “They might be looking for a strategic partner or customers or grant funding. There’s all kinds of ways to scale these businesses.”
The 2027 Data Center Innovation Cohort will be based at the Seattle Climate Innovation Hub downtown.
An information session is set for Oct. 15, and applications are due Nov. 15. The cohort begins in February.

articles.title: From school nuggets to insect kibble: How the next generation of faux meats aims to win over skeptics
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Subscribe to Positive Charge : Apple Podcasts , Spotify , Amazon Music , All Episodes

More than 40 years ago, the first commercial veggie burger made its debut in London markets as packets of dehydrated ingredients that were mixed with water and shaped into patties. Today’s alternative proteins are unrecognizable in comparison, featuring cell-cultivated meats grown in brewery-style stainless steel tanks, fake sushi and faux burgers that “bleed.”

The sector saw a surge in the early 2020s to become a $1 billion market , but enthusiasm has wilted of late. Beyond Meat, for example, has seen its stock plummet following its 2019 IPO, and only 11% of U.S. households purchased faux meat last year.
Yet repeat purchases remain strong, global demand is rising, and academic research as well as entrepreneurial R&D are advancing the field.

“Any new emerging technology always goes through challenges in scaling, economics, [and] consumer acceptance,” said Rohan Shirwaiker , director of the Bezos Center for Sustainable Protein at North Carolina State University . “The trajectory, I think, is in the right direction.”
Alternative proteins fall into three categories, and they can be combined in some products:
Plant-based: Made from ingredients including soy, beans, peas, lentils and wheat.

Fermentation-produced: Uses organisms such as fungi, bacteria, yeast and algae to act as ingredients themselves or as tiny factories producing compounds including proteins found in milk or eggs, or specific fats.
Cell-cultivated meats: Derived from animal cells and grown in nutrient-rich broth, then coaxed into fat or muscle tissue.

Consumers buy alternative proteins because of environmental concerns around climate impacts and the land and water footprint of livestock; health worries about cholesterol and saturated fats; and ethical objections to factory farming. And experts say that as the global population grows, there won’t be enough beef, chicken and fish to meet protein needs.

But there are significant hurdles to adoption. The faux meats are generally more expensive. People are unsure about the technologies used to make the foods. Consumers need to adapt to different flavors and textures and have worries that the alternatives are “ultra-processed” foods.
Rebellyous Foods , a startup churning out faux chicken nuggets for 6 million U.S. school kids, runs its R&D operations out of an office park south of Seattle.

“We want people to feel good about what they eat, and so our products have a relatively short ingredient list,” said Christie Lagally Bradburn , founder and CEO of Rebellyous. That includes soy protein, yeast-based flavoring and salt, oil and water, and a binder called methyl cellulose found in products such as bread and salad dressing.

Despite being derived from plants, the Rebellyous kickin’ nuggets have a meat-like texture absent the gristle and mystery bits. The flavor, Lagally Bradburn said, is often compared to Campbell’s chicken noodle soup. The brand also has spicier options targeting food service at hospitals and correctional facilities.

Lagally Bradburn’s background is in designing manufacturing equipment, including roles at Boeing creating tools to build airplanes faster, better and cheaper. An ethical vegan, she wanted to apply that skill set to replacing meat, and in 2017 she launched Rebellyous to do it. Her goal: an automated, continuously operating system for producing affordable and tasty fake chicken products.

The company developed its Mock 3 system, capable of producing more than 5,000 pounds of faux chicken per hour. The device was installed in a facility north of Seattle, but the operators recently shuttered the site on short notice. So Rebellyous is working with its long-term partner in New Mexico which uses a conventional manufacturing system.
The hope is to find a new home for the Mock 3 while also developing its Mock 4, a smaller, cheaper, simpler device.
“Our goal is to run a financially sound company, to be there for the schools,” Lagally Bradburn said, as well as play a role in addressing climate change, human health and animal welfare issues.

While Rebellyous targets human food service, other startups are focused on four-legged consumers. About a decade ago, Anne Carlson was planning a career change when her daughter shared that she didn’t want children due to climate worries.
“I realized that I couldn’t just do a normal job after that,” she said. “Building a better future for her was everything.”

Carlson, a pet-industry veteran, noted UCLA research showing U.S. pets account for 25% to 30% of the environmental impact of domestic meat consumption. That led her to pursue insects as alternative proteins for pets, starting with crickets, then adding black soldier fly larvae.
In 2020, her company, called Jiminy’s , became the first in the country to be approved by the FDA and an association that regulates animal food standards to sell cricket-based dog foods.

“It’s less land, less water and almost no greenhouse gases,” Carlson said of the bug proteins. One acre of land used to raise 265 pounds of chicken protein will provide 60,000 pounds of cricket protein.

Jiminy’s sells kibble, treats and dental chews that provide essential amino acids and show benefits for dogs with allergies and digestion issues. The products typically cost more than animal-based foods, but are cheaper than prescription diets.
The San Francisco Bay Area startup still has to win over owners who are squeamish about insects — but they needn’t be, Carlson said.
“People think that when they open the bag, it’s going to be a bag full of bugs. It is absolutely not that,” she said. The product looks and smells like typical dog food, so “it’s not scary at all.”
One area of growing concern centers on ultra-processed foods and whether alternative proteins fall under that category.

Shirwaiker, director of the Bezos Center, notes that while some products contain high sodium or fat, processing itself can be beneficial by removing harmful elements, improving texture and preserving nutrition.

“If we are using processing to get the right texture, something that consumers will like without sacrificing the nutrition, I don’t think that’s a bad thing at all,” he said. “So it’s really a matter of perspective and trying to separate process from nutrition in some way.”

Rebellyous and Jiminy’s leaders said they clearly disclose ingredients and keep them simple to put those fears to rest. The biggest hurdle, both said, was bringing down costs while supply-chain prices keep rising.

Even so, the startups are on the verge of profitability, their CEOs said. Carlson said Jiminy’s operates in the black some months and is growing faster than the pet industry overall. Because Rebellyous primarily serves schools, it’s profitable during much of the year, but business slows in the summer, Lagally Bradburn said.
Both founders remain optimistic about the long-term horizon.
“Sometimes when you’re in it, it can be hard to see the forest for the trees,” Lagally Bradburn said. “But the truth is that overall, the world is becoming more sustainable.”

articles.title: Interlune raises $5M for initiatives that go beyond mining the moon
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: Seattle-based Interlune has raised $5 million in fresh funding to support a business plan that involves building space infrastructure as well as mining the moon for helium-3 and other valuable resources.

The funds were raised through a Simple Agreement for Future Equity, or SAFE, in which investors provide upfront cash to a startup in exchange for shares to be issued during a future priced round. Interlune used the same approach to raise $5 million earlier this year .
Interlune said existing and new investors participated in its latest SAFE offering, which came to light today in a regulatory filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

“The company’s continued traction with government contracts, along with major milestones across the space ecosystem over the past year, makes this a beneficial approach ahead of our next priced round,” Interlune CEO Rob Meyerson said in an emailed statement.

When Interlune was founded in 2020, the company focused primarily on developing technologies for extracting resources from lunar rocks and soil, also known as regolith. Helium-3 leads its target list because that material is more abundant on the moon than on Earth and is highly valued for applications ranging from medical imaging and quantum computing to fusion power . The price for helium-3 can exceed $9 million a pound .

Meyerson noted that Interlune’s business plan is no longer limited to space mining. “In response to growing market demand, we’ve expanded our product offering to include space infrastructure and survival services, leveraging the same technologies we’ve been developing to harvest natural resources from space,” he said.

In July, Interlune announced it was expanding its partnership with Vermeer , an Iowa-based industrial equipment manufacturer, to develop construction tools for use on the moon. Such tools could support NASA’s 10-year, $30 billion initiative to build the infrastructure for a moon base. Interlune is also adapting its helium-3 extraction process for terrestrial applications .

The company is planning to send its first payload — a mineralogical mapping instrument — to the moon later this year aboard Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 lander . Follow-up missions will characterize the moon’s helium-3 reserves and test technologies for excavation and extraction . Interlune plans to start harvesting lunar helium-3 and bringing it back to Earth in the 2030s .

articles.title: 206 Burger teaming up with Capitol Hill sports bar Pitch the Baby on 19th Ave E
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Capitol Hill “sports bar for everybody” Pitch the Baby appears to still be in the game but a new food and drink player is joining the 19th Ave E scene.

A few dark nights and unexpected closures caused a few concerns — and emails to CHS — but the sports bar was open and serving this week as the Mariners spent their evenings sinking another season. The change is coming next door where signage has gone up announcing a new Pitch the Baby neighbor.
206 Burger Company is set to move in next door and revive the space adjoining the sports bar that has struggled to find its footing.
CHS reported early this year as Pitch the Baby expanded into the other half of the long ago Kingfish Cafe space as the Monica Dimas -backed Tortas Condesa venture was consolidated.

A half-year and 82 Mariners losses later and Pitch the Baby appears ready to downsize and reduce its footprint to the main bar space of the old Kingfish. We’ve asked Dimas and the rest of the Pitch the Baby partnership for details but have not heard back.
206 Burger owner Suren Shretha , meanwhile, tells us there will be more information soon on the link up.
Pitch the Baby debuted in late summer 2025 as Rocket Taco moved across the street to its new home on the southeast side of 19th and Mercer.

This will be the third 206 Burger location. In 2024, Shretha and the small chain took over the former 8 Oz. burger bar location at Broadway and Union as the Nepal-born burger entrepreneur gets his plans of careful expansion back on track after the economic bumps of the pandemic.
206 Burger is getting ready to open at 602 19th Ave E. Follow @206burgercompany for updates.

articles.title: Wilson taps Seattle CARE Department as command center in new gun violence plan
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Police place evidence markers after a July shootout on 11th Ave that injured bystanders caught in the crossfire

Seattle’s mayor has unveiled her budget plan to address shootings in the city that would make the CARE Department the central command center for gun violence reduction, focusing $13 million in spending on the city’s emergency response system and human services to power a new approach that integrates Seattle’s 9-1-1 resources with community responses and intervention teams.

Mayor Katie Wilson unveiled her administration’s gun violence reduction plan this week designating the Community Assisted Response and Engagement Department as a new central command center to take on the public safety priority.

The goal, Wilson says, is for Seattle City Hall to take “faster action when shootings occur.” The result is a possible new direction for the city that would focus new energy — and spending — on community public safety and intervention resources at CARE and not with traditional policing at the Seattle Police Department .

“Together, these efforts aim to give the city stronger regulatory authority, reinforce youth focused safety programs, and improve protections for neighborhoods experiencing persistent harm,” the plan reads.

According to the plan, the mayor’s proposed 2027 budget will include transferring “$5 million Community Violence Intervention contracts with nine organizations, from the Human Services Department to CARE,” moving the community violence interrupters into the 9-1-1 emergency response system to pair frontline teams with 9-1-1 dispatch, the Seattle Police Department, and the Seattle Fire Department .

These contracted services include hospital-based support for gunshot victims and their families in partnership with Harborview Medical Center , place-based work focused on “outreach, conflict mediation, hotspot stabilization, and incident recovery,” and individual interventions directed at the “small subset of individuals involved in the majority of gun violence.”

The plan would also include the creation of a new Director of Gun Violence Reduction role at CARE funded in 2026 and a new coordinator added in the 2027 budget to oversee and manage operations. Alongside new personnel, the proposed 2027–2028 budget expands CARE’s Community Crisis Response working hours by 85%, increasing service from 10 hours to “over 18 hours per day” with daily operational hours running from 6:30 AM to 1:00 AM.

The plan also integrates legal enforcement tools with CARE’s community-level deployment. The mayor proposes maintaining a 2026 investment in a dedicated attorney inside Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans’ office to file civil Extreme Risk Protection Order petitions. This attorney will review violent crime intelligence, retaliation threats, and witness intimidation alongside SPD to remove firearms from individuals presenting significant community danger, focusing on Rainier Beach, Aurora Avenue, and Belltown.

The Wilson plan does not lean heavily on traditional policing. One area of SPD investment would be spending on increased bicycle patrols including across gun violence hot spots, while taking preliminary steps toward a “focused deterrence approach in coordination with CARE and trusted community partners.”

The mayor’s plan would mark a significant expansion of the CARE Department and Chief Amy Barden’s role. CHS reported here on CARE’s crisis responders’ expanded hours of service even as Barden says she is continuing to guide the department to overcome limitations placed on its responders by the Seattle Police Department. Barden says CARE crisis responders remain hamstrung and sidelined by the new contract with the Seattle Police Officers Guild union and that SPD’s approach has limited CARE responses.

Wilson’s proposal comes as business leaders and officials including District 3 representative Joy Hollingsworth have criticized her administration’s approach to public safety and called for an emergency “100-day plan” to address shootings and street disorder in the city. Hollingsworth and the coalition of regional CEOs say low officer totals, slow 911 response times, and the stalled expansion of SPD’s Real Time Crime Center camera system as issues that require immediate response and cites an August Chamber survey where only 34% of 500 registered voters expressed confidence in Seattle’s public safety approach.

The business coalition’s public safety push arrives as Wilson faces a looming budget deficit while prioritizing civilian alternatives, harm reduction, and administrative accountability over traditional police expansion — forcing out Chief Shon Barnes , targeting hotspot patrols, and freezing surveillance camera expansion.

Recent weeks have also brought a burst of gun violence including a man shot and killed, and three others injured in a shooting at Denny and 4th Ave, a woman shot and killed near 3rd and Blanchard, and a 17-year-old shot and killed near Elliott and Bell . Meanwhile, police investigated bullet damage to vehicles after a burst of gunfire left no injuries at 22nd and Jackson — all on the same weekend.

Despite the burst, officials say gun violence continues to trend lower in Seattle and King County. The latest report from King County Prosecuting Attorney showed the first quarter of 2026 marked a new milestone in the return to safer levels coming out of the pandemic as deadly shootings dropped to “single digits” for the first time in nine years. In the first three months of the year, the county recorded nine “gun violence homicides,” the lowest mark since 2017.

Still, shooting deaths and gun violence continue and community groups including Capitol Hill and First Hill’s Circle the Blocks are calling for more to be done to address gun violence hot spots in the city.

Broader prevention measures in the Wilson plan include over $8 million in ongoing Human Services investments and more than $600,000 allocated to Rainier Beach High School for after-school programming and peer mentorship.
The mayor is also planning academic partnerships.

Under the mayor’s plan, the University of Washington’s Center for Firearm Injury Prevention will map existing data and service gaps, while the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions will help launch Seattle’s first Violence Reduction Council to conduct multidisciplinary action reviews of every homicide to “identify where systems and services failed and correct them so similar homicides don’t occur again.”

Wilson’s plan does not include a contract with the National Network for Safe Communities research center called for by Councilmember Maritza Rivera and her counterparts setting up another potential battle with the council as it takes up the mayor’s complete budget proposal when it is unveiled next week.

articles.title: Seattle Breaks Ground on West Seattle RV Safe Lot
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Last Thursday, the Low Income Housing Institute (LIHI) hosted a groundbreaking ceremony for Seattle's Glassyard Commons, a new RV safe lot near South Park that is intended to provide another pathway out of homelessness and into stable housing.

The facility will feature parking for 72 recreational vehicles (RVs) and 20 tiny houses on 3.9-acre site that LIHI is leasing from the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT). The triangular parcel is hemmed in by 2nd Avenue SW and W Marginal Way SW and located just south of the 1st Avenue S bridge over the Duwamish River. LIHI expects Glassyard Commons to open by mid-November and serve 140 people.

The WSDOT property had been considered as a site for transitional housing during a previous mayoral administration , according to reporting from the West Seattle Blog, but ultimately moved forward quickly after Katie Wilson took office promising to add 1,000 shelter beds within her first year in office. This week, Wilson scaled back that plan to a more achievable 1,000 beds by the end of 2027 .
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

At the groundbreaking, LIHI Executive Director Sharon Lee emphasized that the lot is intended to serve people who are homeless – and that surrendering their vehicle once they're permanently housed is part of the bargain.

"There could be as many as 300, 400 RVs [across Seattle]," Lee said. "Not all of them will want to come into the safe lot because part of the requirement for the safe lot is that they consider moving into housing. Not that they, you know, just hang out here, right? This is not just a parking place for people traveling through Seattle. This is for people who have no home except to survive in a RV, and oftentimes the RVs are pretty derelict, rundown, and unsafe."

Lee said these rundown RVs pose a public health risk. Councilmember Dan Strauss, who was not at the event, has also raised the issue and proposed legislation ramping up enforcement on illegally parked RVs, including seizure of non-compliant vehicles. In order to be admitted to the safe lot, RVs will be drained of fuel and electrified, with the ultimate goal of transitioning its residents into a different form of housing.

“People die living in dilapidated RVs because they are dangerous and can catch on fire. Far too many people are trying to survive in RVs because they don’t have access to housing they can afford," Lee said. "Glassyard Commons will create pathways to stable housing and will help remove hundreds of RVs off the streets of Seattle.”

As of last week, the site consisted largely of gravel and markers showing where structures will be placed. Construction has already begun on a concrete pad for a shared kitchen and utilities for the RV spaces, Lee said.
The City of Seattle, through the Human Services Department (HSD), will be providing $3.3 million in annual funding to support operations on site.

“My top priority is getting people inside with quality shelter and access to services," Mayor Katie Wilson said in a statement. "Every person experiencing homelessness has their own unique hurdles we need to help them overcome, and it is important to provide a range of types of shelter and services. Glassyard Commons will provide a personalized approach for individuals living in unsafe and unhealthy RVs, giving them a path to the help they need and permanent housing.”

Glassyard Commons will feature a staffed entry pavilion, 24/7 staff, case management offices, a community kitchen, and hygiene and laundry facilities, LIHI said. "On-site case managers will support participants with obtaining identification, employment, health and behavioral health services, education, and housing navigation."

Councilmember Bob Kettle (District 7) stressed that RV lots fit well into a public safety response. During a recent City Council meeting, Kettle claimed that unsupervised pods of RVs often become magnets for illegal activity, like drug dealing and trafficking in stolen goods. Kettle has become one of the mayor's biggest critics in recent weeks, particularly when it comes to issues surrounding the Seattle Police Department, but in this case aligned himself fairly directly with Wilson's overall goals for increasing shelter capacity.
“When we have a big collection of RVs, oftentimes one starts dealing drugs and we have a drug market,” Kettle said. “And once you have a drug market, you have a stolen goods market.”
At the ceremony, Kettle noted his advocacy for the Salmon Bay Village , a former RV safe lot in Interbay, which provided a template on which Glassyard Commons was modeled.

"I saw it very directly before I became a councilmember, as someone in the community that was engaged," Kettle said. "I was working this really hard in terms of the Salmon Bay Village project, and I saw how it worked. I saw the work that LIHI put in in terms of community outreach, for example, with the Magnolia Community Council and other groups, but then also implementing the lessons learned [...] having the counselor there to work with the people to break that emotional link between the RV, and then moving on to housing. That is so key."
When The Urbanist asked if he supports Strauss's RV legislation, Kettle demurred, saying the package of bills had to work its way through the committee process.

"At the end of the day, we have to get to a place where we're doing right for those that are in crisis, our neighbors, but also for our neighborhoods," Kettle said. "And I'm looking for that balance, and basically looking to address the seam that exists between traditional public safety, but also the public health, housing, and services."

In its press release, LIHI has stressed that getting unsafe RVs off Seattle streets is key part of their mission: "The goal of Glassyard Commons is to encourage vehicle residents to leave their rundown RVs, move temporarily into the safe lot or a tiny house, and work with case managers to obtain permanent housing. Once housing is secured, the RVs are demolished and disposed of by LIHI at no cost to the participants. This prevents the RVs from being recirculated back onto the streets of Seattle."
Brian Nielson, WSDOT's regional administrator for Northwest Region, spoke at the event, highlighting that encampments encroaching on highway right-of-way have been an issue for the state.

"We need to be clear about transportation: It's not a safe place to live," Nielson said. "The areas are designed for highways and transportation infrastructure. Living there puts people close to traffic and other hazards. They do not provide the basic infrastructure and services that people need to live safely. This is why Glassyard Commons matters. WSDOT is providing the property, but LIHI and their partners are creating something much more important: a place where people have safety and stability, access to services and case management, and the opportunity to work toward permanent housing. This is what partnership should look like."

The auditory experience of the groundbreaking made clear that while the safe lot won't be located directly on highway right-of-way, it's still sandwiched into a busy trucking corridor with plenty of loud traffic going by. Amenities are scant in the industrial area, although the nautically themed Mighty Mugs Coffee Shop and a truck stop Subway sandwich shop are about a 10-minute walk away. The lot is close to a bus stop.

LIHI had been working with WSDOT for a long time to find surplus land that could work for a project, Lee said. Given the large amount of space they need and the potential for complaints from neighbors, RV safe lots have largely been sited in industrial areas.

Referrals for spots at Glassyard will be made from outreach workers contracted through the HSD. Preference will be given to Council District 1 and other locations with large numbers of RVs, LIHI noted.
HSD Director Tanya Kim noted that more shelter expansions and tiny home villages were on the way.

"The City is investing in two more tiny home villages, a master leased shelter, and two shelter expansions that are scheduled to open at the end of this year and at the beginning of next year," Kim said. "So there is much more coming, and they're diversified."

“Glassyard Commons is a proven concept offering safe RV parking and is modeled after the success of Salmon Bay Village RV Safe Lot in Interbay," Jeffrey said. "Over a short period of time 67 RVs were taken off city streets and destroyed and 89 people, including five homeless veterans, received services, shelter or housing to exit homelessness.”
On Thursday, a New Hope church member named Erica also delivered the clearest call to action of the program, urging Seattle to invest even more in the social safety net to lift more out of poverty.

"Dr. Martin Luther King says any religion that professes to be concerned about the souls of men, humans, and not concerned about the slums that damn them, the economic conditions that strangle them, and the social conditions that cripple them is a spiritually morbid religion awaiting burial," Erica said. Melania didn’t accompany her husband on the trip (“Uh, she sends her regards,” Trump said), but his devoted aide Natalie Harp was obviously at his side.

You’ll know Harp: the 35-year-old assistant was headline news last month after Democratic senator Jon Ossoff quipped that Trump didn’t want to do his job; he just wanted to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie”. That comment would have been quickly forgotten were it not for the Trump administration’s unhinged response (sample: “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics”), which sparked a media frenzy. Orville Peck was in the middle of a soundcheck when he found out that his idol Dolly Parton had died. It was late August and the masked, pseudonymous country singer was due to perform an intimate set at London’s Rough Trade East in half an hour. The news hit him like a truck. With no chance to process it, he decided to grieve in real time, on stage, before a roomful of fans.

“I’m a little bit of a mess right now,” Peck told the audience, perched on a stool with an acoustic guitar. “Dolly was my hero,” he continued, his voice cracking. “As a gay man coming into country music and feeling sort of alone, I think the thing that always felt comforting is, like, just knowing Dolly existed in country. It made me feel like I had a friend there.” He then launched into a rendition of Parton’s iconic hit I Will Always Love You.

Horne had started getting into character at 5am, for a makeup and clown-costuming process that would take two hours. It would be another 10 hours before Horne was allowed to address the city council about the passing of Romanch’s Law, which would phase out and ultimately ban New York’s horse carriage industry.

From the moment Horne walked into the meeting room, carriage horse proponents ridiculed them, pointing and laughing. Dressed in a black top hat and gloves with their face painted white and red, Horne began their three-minute speech : “We pride ourselves on being a world-class destination … yet we are clinging to the exploitation of horse-drawn carriages. A giant prey animal is not built to thrive in New York’s overstimulating concrete environment.” Horne later learned that those carriage horse supporters went on social media to poke fun at their display. “They fell right into my trap,” Horne said. “They decided to critique the messenger and not the message.”

articles.title: If you’re on GLP-1 drugs and plan to fast for Yom Kippur, here’s what you need to know
articles.author:
<name>Reed Berger-Fleishman, Associate Clinical Professor of Medicine and Surgery, University of Illinois Chicago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/reed-berger-fleishman-2764205"/>
paras: Millions of people worldwide – as many as 1 in 8 adults in the U.S. – are on GLP-1 medication, such as Ozempic, Mounjaro, Wegovy and Zepbound, for treating diabetes or for weight loss.

These drugs are adding a medical twist to religious observances that involve fasting, such as the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, which will be observed from sundown on Sept. 20 until nightfall on Sept. 21, 2026. Traditionally, fasting on Yom Kippur means forgoing food and water for about 25 hour, which can strongly affect a person’s metabolism.

Other religious traditions include different types of fasts. For example, Muslims who fast during Ramadan neither eat nor drink from dawn to sunset, but they break their fast each night. Christian and Hindu traditions also include dry fasts as well as partial fasts, such as Lent and Navratri , in which people avoid certain foods.

As a specialist in obesity medicine , I work with many patients who take GLP-1 drugs. Most people can safely fast for Yom Kippur or other religious or cultural observances. But depending on their circumstances, they may need to plan ahead, take certain precautions and be clear on when it’s medically advised that they break their fast.

GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic, Mounjaro, Wegovy and Zepbound mimic a natural gut hormone – glucagon-like peptide 1 – that lowers your blood sugar by triggering insulin release when your blood sugar is high. These drugs also slow how quickly food passes through the stomach, which reduces appetite to aid in weight loss .

GLP-1s have some common side effects that can occur in anyone taking them, including nausea, vomiting, dizziness, constipation and dehydration. Fasting may exacerbate them , especially in people who are prone to an upset stomach. GLP-1 side effects are also more common when a patient is increasing their dose, which usually happens monthly as tolerated until they reach their full dosage.
That’s why, if you’re planning to fast for Yom Kippur, it’s best to avoid starting a new GLP-1 medication or increasing the dose of your medication sooner than two weeks or so before the holiday.

If you take GLP-1 drugs as weekly injections, which is the most common way of dosing these medications, you should stick to your schedule even if you plan to fast. These drugs stay in your system during the entire week, so moving or skipping that weekly dose right before fasting can interfere with their effects on blood sugar or weight loss.

If your weekly injection falls on Yom Kippur, you can generally go ahead and administer it as scheduled. Some patients do report increased nausea on their injection day – if that happens to you, you may wish to delay the injection until after the fast, if you’ve cleared it with your doctor.

Patients who inject GLP-1 drugs daily may need to adjust the timing. For patients taking these medications for diabetes treatment, it may make sense to do the injection right before the meal that breaks the fast or to hold off until after the fast. This helps reduce the risk of stomach side effects, which can occur when these medications are taken on an empty stomach.

More recently, many patients have switched to oral GLP-1 medications . These pills must generally be taken on an empty stomach with a small amount of water, at a set time before taking any other drugs or any food or beverages.

Because fasting for Yom Kippur includes abstaining from drinking, taking the pill as directed may involve breaking the fast. That means you’ll need to decide in advance whether to take the medicine before the fast begins, after the fast ends or on an alternative schedule. It’s best to avoid simply skipping the daily dose scheduled for Yom Kippur and taking a double dose after the fast.

Skipping the dose won’t be harmful if you’re taking the medication for weight loss. But if you have diabetes, skipping it could dangerously elevate your blood sugar. And doubling the dose later could lead to serious side effects, such as pancreatitis, an inflammation of the pancreas that can lead to hospitalization.

If you’re using GLP-1 medications solely for weight management, fasting for 25 hours should not pose serious issues beyond stomach upset. In rare cases, though, combining these drugs with fasting can stress the pancreas enough to cause pancreatitis .

Fasting on GLP-1s carries the biggest risks for diabetic patients. That’s because GLP-1 medications are often used alongside other drugs that work primarily by lowering blood sugar, which raises patients’ overall risk of a blood sugar crash.

The greatest concern is in patients taking a GLP-1 medication together with insulin or drugs that stimulate insulin production, such as sulfonylureas . The GLP-1 medication itself may not cause a drop in blood sugar. But because it suppresses appetite and lowers glucose levels, these other medications can magnify the risk of low blood sugar during a prolonged fast.
If that’s your situation, talk to your doctor about whether you can adjust the timing, dose and type of insulin you take and reduce your dose of sulfonylurea in order to fast safely.
In general, people who have Type 1 diabetes or poorly controlled diabetes are strongly advised not to fast – as are people who:
Regardless of what GLP-1 medication you take and for what indication, if you plan to fast you’ll need to do some pregaming, monitor how your fast is going and be mindful of how you break it.

First, if you are unsure about anything, talk to the clinician who is monitoring your GLP-1 drug treatment so you can decide together whether fasting is safe for you and whether your situation requires any special precautions.

Before fasting, it’s important to eat a normal meal that includes protein and to avoid both overeating and undereating. Overeating is never recommended when on GLP-1 medications , and undereating can set you up for more side effects during the fast . Although GLP-1 therapy can substantially reduce appetite, patients should avoid skipping the prefast meal entirely.

GLP-1 medications don’t just decrease appetite – they can also suppress the body’s natural thirst signals . So before your fast begins, aim to stay hydrated to prevent getting dehydrated while fasting.

If you are diabetic, make sure you fast under close guidance from your doctor – and make sure you are checking your blood sugar during fasting. Using a glucose monitor is a good idea, particularly if you are taking insulin or other glucose-lowering medications. The goal is for your blood sugar to remain within your usual daily nonfasting range.

Be ready to break your fast right away if you start feeling dizzy, confused, faint, nauseated or acutely ill, or if your blood sugar dips too low or spikes too high. These symptoms are dangerous and need to be addressed immediately. Stash a rapid source of carbohydrates – even just some glucose tablets or a few hard candies – within reach so you can access them quickly if needed.

Finally, plan a gentle, balanced meal to break the fast rather than an unusually large meal, which may provoke nausea, abdominal pain, reflux or vomiting. It’s generally best to avoid higher-fat foods, too, since they can slow down digestion.

articles.title: Rapid Houthi advances in Yemen pose massive strategic risks for Saudi Arabia in the Gulf
articles.author:
<name>Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, Fellow for the Middle East at the Baker Institute, Rice University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/kristian-coates-ulrichsen-128169"/>
paras: An advance by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, which has included the targeting of Saudi cities and infrastructure , has quickly complicated a widening Middle East war.

Not only has it all but unraveled a 2022 truce putting a lid on Yemen’s civil war – in which the Iran-aligned Houthis were fighting a Saudi-led coalition – but the seizure of territory next to the Red Sea has further threatened Saudi energy exports. On Sept. 13, Saudi Arabia and other Arab Gulf nations were due to take part in crucial Omani-hosted talks with Iran in a bid to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. But they were called off , seemingly over attacks by both the Houthis and Iraqi groups aligned with Tehran.
The Conversation spoke with Gulf analyst Kristian Coates Ulrichsen to help make sense of the dizzying array of intersecting news developments.

Periodically since the war in Iran began on Feb. 28 , 2026, and particularly since the signing of the Iran-U.S. memorandum of understanding in mid-June , Omani and Iranian officials have been meeting to discuss how to resolve the blockage in the Strait of Hormuz.

Oman and Iran are the two coastal Gulf States through which the waterway passes, despite Iranian rhetoric about securing and maintaining control over the strait. The challenges facing the negotiators is that Oman will need to build consensus among the other Gulf States for any agreement, as well as the United States, given that one Iranian demand is for passage to be limited to civilian vessels, which would effectively bar U.S. naval ships from the Gulf, including the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, which is headquartered in Bahrain.

Gulf officials – and their U.S. counterparts – would strenuously resist any Iranian attempt to convert their wartime leverage over the strait into a postwar deal that formalizes and regularizes that control.

The postponement of the planned meeting in Oman’s capital Muscat illustrates that the time is not yet right for the talks to proceed and that further dialogue is needed in order to build a consensual framework that can best enable them to succeed.
The uptick in attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure has put in jeopardy the viability of the work-around to Hormuz that enabled the kingdom to maintain oil exports at about half their prewar levels.

Saudi vessels have already started to avoid transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and taking the far longer route through the Suez Canal into the Mediterranean and around the coast of Africa. That adds weeks and associated costs to oil exports to predominantly Asian markets.

While the damage to a pumping station that led to the temporary closure of the Saudi’s East-West Pipeline was reportedly done by a drone launched from Iraq, the kingdom faces attacks from both its northern and southern neighbors with the range, intent and capability to hit critical energy targets.

Saudi officials may respond to the latest attacks by rerouting oil back to its east coast facilities on the Persian Gulf, and there has been a steady increase in the volume of oil making its way through Hormuz in recent days and weeks. This return to using the Saudi port at Ras Tanura nevertheless makes oil transportation remain vulnerable to Iranian attacks on shipping in the strait.

Moreover, should the Saudis face a “double choke point” crisis whereby the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait are both effectively shut, there will be no safe and secure way to continue Saudi oil and other industrial exports, or the import of non-oil goods and commodities by ship.

Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in Yemen in March 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition but quickly got bogged down in an unwinnable conflict. In fact, the major successes in ground operations against the Houthis and other adversaries in Yemen were achieved by the United Arab Emirates rather than Saudi forces.

There is very little appetite in Riyadh for a new military operation in Yemen, especially since the Houthis are skilled in asymmetric combat and have far more advanced drone and other technological capabilities than they possessed during the previous rounds of conflict with Saudi Arabia.

The fact that the Houthis outlasted the two-month U.S. Operation Rough Rider between March and May 2025 indicates that bombing from the air will not force the Houthis into submission. And the rapid advance made by the Houthis to take Mokha and other positions in southwestern Yemen since Sept. 3 suggest that Saudi-trained forces on the ground are insufficient.

The Saudi leadership, led by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman , is instead seeking to put together a multilateral coalition of states that may be able to contribute, in different ways, to ensuring maritime and regional security in and around the Red Sea. This will include the recent signatories Pakistan and Turkey, alongside Saudi Arabia, to the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and may also include Egypt, which Crown Prince Mohammed visited on Sept. 15 .
Egypt and Turkey may be able to contribute naval assets to assist with maritime patrols in the Red Sea, while Pakistan has long provided Saudi Arabia with soldiers to help protect the kingdom.

Saudi officials, along with counterparts in other Gulf States, urged the U.S. and Iran to reach a diplomatic resolution prior to the launch of the war on Feb. 28 and have found themselves caught in the middle of a conflict they sought to avoid.
The perception that the U.S. began the war without a “Plan B” has intersected with the feeling that the U.S. has done little to protect Saudi Arabia and the other Gulf States.

If the White House continues to struggle to make progress in negotiating an end to the war and a resumption of unrestricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz , it may be that regional states step in to make a deal of their own. The postponement of the Oman meeting suggests we are not yet at that point. Yet patience may certainly be wearing thin in Riyadh.

articles.title: Pardoned by Trump and escaping charges at home, ex-Honduran leader’s case shows a nation’s struggle for sovereignty
articles.author:
<name>Laura Blume, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Nevada, Reno</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/laura-blume-2525066"/>
paras: A Honduran judge on Sept. 1, 2026, dismissed a sprawling money-laundering and fraud case against the country’s former president, Juan Orlando Hernández. It was the latest stroke of good fortune for Hernández.

Hernández returned home in late July after an eventful four years outside Honduras. He was extradited to the United States in 2022 following a multiyear, nonpartisan U.S. investigation . In 2024 he was convicted of cocaine trafficking and related charges and sentenced to 45 years behind bars in the U.S . Yet after serving only 18 months of his sentence, Hernández was pardoned by President Donald Trump .
Hernández remains a forceful power broker behind the scenes of the current Honduran government, led by President Nasry Asfura of the right-wing National Party.

Yet as a scholar of Latin American politics , I believe Hernández’s return to Honduras, and his successes evading legal accountability, are emblematic of something broader than impunity for elites: His case demonstrates the struggle for sovereignty in a country facing a renewed form of U.S. intervention.

Hernández’s return to Honduras on July 26 was symbolic. He landed at Palmerola International Airport, which shares its runway with the Soto Cano Air Base, a longtime staging ground of U.S. interventions in Honduras.
While Hernández was greeted by National Party supporters , for many Hondurans his pardon and return to the country were seen to undermine hopes for justice and adversely affect the political process.

When Trump first announced plans to pardon Hernández , it was on the eve of the Honduran elections in November 2025. In another sign of meddling from Washington, Trump endorsed Asfura and threatened to cut off aid to Honduras if Asfura, who was trailing in opinion polls leading up to the elections , did not win.

On Dec. 1, the day after the election and with Asfura and center-right politician Salvador Nasralla locked in a technical tie as vote counting continued, Trump issued a full pardon for Hernández. U.S. officials then hurried to provide special immigration protections for Hernández, and a specialized tactical team drove him from a West Virginia prison to the luxury Waldorf Astoria hotel in Manhattan.

Back in Honduras, the pardon was seen as a “ green light for the National Party to manipulate the vote ,” as a former high-ranking U.S. diplomat told ProPublica. Trump’s actions signaled that Washington supported the National Party’s engagement in electoral manipulation, as election observers and academic experts say happened in 2017 with Hernández’s unconstitutional second presidential term election.
Following weeks of suspicious delays and fraud allegations , Asfura was announced the winner on Dec. 24, 2025 , by a margin of less than 1 percent.
Although free from the U.S. justice system, Hernández still potentially faced charges in Honduras.
On Dec. 9 the Honduran attorney general reactivated an international arrest warrant for Hernández over charges of fraud and money laundering.

These charges are part of the corruption case known as Pandora , a scheme that embezzled $12 million in public funding and allegedly diverted that money into political campaigns , including Hernández’s 2013 presidential campaign.

Previous Pandora trials accused major National Party figures , yet during Hernández’s presidency a special appeals court dismissed the cases . But under the left-leaning administration of Xiomara Castro – from 2022 to 2026 – Honduras in 2023 indicted former National Party presidents Hernández and his predecessor, Porfirio Lobo.

Hernández remained in the U.S. until his international arrest warrant was suspended, returning to Honduras shortly before his initial trial . On Aug. 12, 2026, the Public Ministry confirmed the charges against Hernández and presented 48 pieces of evidence . Yet after two weeks, the court dropped the charges against Hernández .

With the National Party back in power , few believed Hernández could be held accountable in Honduras, particularly given that the Honduran judicial system is plagued by targeted violence that undermines the rule of law.
Indeed, impunity is virtually guaranteed for the wealthy and powerful. And that is something Hernández helped ensure.

Under his presidency, Honduras passed legal reforms specifically reducing sentences for money laundering and protecting politicians from investigations for embezzlement . Foreshadowing the likely outcome of Hernández’s trial, Lobo was acquitted days before Hernández’s return.
Although Hernández’s trial is over, controversy over his return remains. That’s in part because of explosive new allegations that surfaced in May 2026.

The Spanish media outlet Canal Red released 37 audio messages allegedly with the voices of politicians, including Asfura and Hernández. According to the leaked audio files, a scandal known as HondurasGate , Hernández’s return was merely one part of an international scheme to undermine left-wing Latin American governments and expand foreign militarization in Honduras.

Those implicated dismiss the files as AI-generated propaganda. While independent analysis suggests the files are likely authentic , valid suspicions from independent sources have emerged casting doubt on their veracity.
Regardless of the HondurasGate audios’ authenticity, much of what they outline echoes wider concerns over external pressures reshaping the region’s politics and expanding militarization.

Trump has been open about seeking to secure right-wing allies throughout the Americas . Weeks after pardoning Hernández’s narco-trafficking, the Trump administration raided Venezuela to arrest President Nicolás Maduro on alleged narco-trafficking charges.

Meanwhile, the U.S. continues to use sanctions in Cuba in an aggressive push for regime change on the island , and has used varying degrees of influence to try to affect elections in places from Colombia to Brazil .
In Honduras, the National Party – and especially Hernández – has been a willing partner in tying its own national priorities to those of the U.S. and close U.S. allies, including Israel.

Hernández cultivated strategic importance as an ally of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Trump. Israel and the U.S. have long provided military technology and security aid to Honduras, and both are expanding military involvement there.

Recently, Honduras signed a memorandum expanding defense cooperation with Israel , and U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced agreements for joint military operations on Honduran, Colombian and Guatemalan soil, similar to ones in Ecuador .

The motivation behind Trump’s support for Asfura’s election and Hernández’s return is also related to advancing controversial charter zones in Honduras known as ZEDEs, the Spanish acronym for Zones for Employment and Economic Development.
Trump allies in Silicon Valley, including Peter Thiel of PayPal and Palantir , are leading investors in Próspera , one of the ZEDEs.

Passed in 2013 under Hernández, the ZEDEs are a highly contested sociopolitical experiement; they create spaces of privatized governance within Honduras that essentially forfeit Honduran sovereignty to U.S. tech titans seeking havens from government regulations and oversight.

The ZEDEs were deemed unconstitutional under the Castro administration, leading Próspera’s billionaire investors to sue Honduras for nearly $11 billion. Now, with the National Party back in power, a renewed corporate push is underway and the ZEDEs are moving forward rapidly, including in Afro-Indigenous territories .

Ultimately, Hernández’s case shows the extent to which a right-wing vision is currently winning in Honduras and, from critics’ standpoint, the risks that vision poses to democratic governance and sovereignty.

As foreign corporations and billionaires secure access to Honduran resources, average Hondurans are struggling. There have been massive politicized layoffs in the public sector . Doctors in the public health system report going months without pay since President Asfura, who also named himself secretary of health , entered office. Meanwhile, private healthcare and agribusiness have received multimillion-dollar government contracts .

At the same time, ongoing U.S. immigration crackdowns are hurting the Honduran economy , which is heavily dependent on remittances. While Hernández remained in the U.S. until he was safe to return to Honduras, the same is not true for thousands of Hondurans who are being deported, often despite fears of violence .
Yet while ordinary Hondurans face rising insecurity, including increasing homicides and disappearances , a special unit of Honduran forces was designated to protect Hernández.
That’s the privileged political environment Hernández spent his career building – and from which he again directly benefits back in Honduras.
