articles.title: Even the Buddha experienced challenges with meditation: Historical texts reveal its potential downsides
articles.author:
<name>Pierce Salguero, Professor of Asian History & Health Humanities, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/pierce-salguero-344686"/>
paras: As a scholar of “ Buddhist medicine ,” I have studied the connections between Buddhism and well-being since the late 1990s. During the course of that research, I would periodically run into sources claiming that meditation could sometimes have unexpected or adverse health effects. When I discovered in 2020 that psychologists were beginning to document the same thing, I began to examine more systematically how Buddhist texts address this issue.

I started coordinating a team of colleagues who translate Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese and other languages to gather sources from around the Buddhist world, which we published in a 2026 book, “ Meditation Sickness: A Sourcebook on the Dangers of Buddhist Practice .” We included scriptures and historical documents but also autobiographies of sufferers and advice from contemporary teachers from across Asia.

What emerges from these collections is the certainty that Buddhism had never understood meditation to be without its dangers. However, the sources also contain potentially valuable advice for what to do when meditation goes wrong.

Decades of scientific research have established the health benefits of mindfulness and other meditation practices, making them a ubiquitous part of today’s global wellness industry. But some researchers have been questioning whether meditation is necessarily safe for everyone. Starting in 2017, psychologist Willoughby Britton , religion scholar Jared Lindahl and their team of researchers at Brown University have documented cases of meditation leading to harm rather than wellness.

Their study, titled The Varieties of Contemplative Experience , involved in-depth interviews with nearly 100 Western Buddhist practitioners and teachers who experienced difficulties – including fear, anxiety, panic, paranoia and other negative experiences – while engaging in different meditation practice traditions.
Other studies have reported similar findings, suggesting that between 3% and 65% of practitioners may experience adverse effects from mindfulness or other forms of contemplative practice.

Meanwhile, Asian Buddhist traditions have been talking about the potential dangers of meditation for millennia. One common name for meditation-related challenges in East Asia has been “ meditation sickness ” – “chanbing” in Chinese, or “zenbyō” in Japanese. They are also commonly diagnosed as disorders of “wind” – “loong” in Tibetan, “lom” in Thai.

Some historical texts describe the Buddha’s own challenges with meditation. In a Pali text commonly dated to the early centuries C.E. called the Great Discourse to Saccaka , for example, the Buddha recounts experiencing headaches and other symptoms as a result of overconcentration.

Many other sources describe similar experiences happening to other people. Secret Essentials for Curing Meditation Sickness , a fifth-century scripture from the Silk Roads kingdom of Khotan, narrates how adept meditators “went mad” when loud sounds startled them while deep in meditation.

Two major scriptures – the Sanskrit Perfection of Insight in 8,000 Lines from the first to second century C.E., and the Chinese Shurangama Sutra , from the eighth century C.E – relate how advanced spiritual practitioners can be vulnerable to attack by “demons.” Whether such demons are understood as external entities or as psychological manifestations is a matter of interpretation in Buddhist traditions.

One story from the Samyukta Agama , dating to the early centuries C.E. and available in multiple languages, even tells of monks who committed suicide en masse after practicing a meditation the Buddha had taught, prompting him to modify his instructions.

One clear takeaway from these Asian Buddhist perspectives on meditation is that side effects are no one’s fault; they are the acknowledged risks of a powerful set of transformative practices. But they are also manageable. While Buddhist sources point out the potential dangers of meditation, many also describe what to do when things go wrong.

Meditation masters and physicians from across Asia have devoted substantial attention to diagnosing and treating practice-related illness with different types of counterbalancing meditations, visualization, chanting, acupuncture, herbs and other remedies. One common type of treatment involves “grounding,” or redirecting attention to the lower abdomen, the feet, or a point deep in the ground below the body.

Another type of grounding involves visualizing energy descending through the body from head to toe. A 17th-century Japanese monk named Hakuin Ekaku, for example, describes visualizing butter melting on the crown of the head and slowly oozing downward, relaxing everything it touches until it reaches the ground.

Whether this accumulated wisdom about how to deal with the side effects of Buddhist practice can be translated into forms useful for contemporary practitioners remains an open question for scholarly study. Addressing this question is a priority of the Contemplative Challenges Collective , a research initiative that I launched earlier this year.

Asian Buddhist traditions also stress that it is crucial to distinguish between the normal healthy challenges of doing something transformative on the one hand and a true medical crisis on the other. In fact, Buddhist texts say that people can expect challenges to arise as part of the process of spiritual development.
Navigating difficult psychological territory – especially encountering one’s traumas and core fears – can be quite difficult and also tremendously rewarding at the same time.

My research shows that Buddhist cultures differ on what crosses a line from expected challenges to debilitating mental and physical conditions. What constitutes a health crisis in ancient India or medieval China is different from 18th-century Japan or 21st-century Tibet. What is tolerable in a community of monastics dedicated to deep contemplative practice will be different from what is reasonable for everyday people interested in stress reduction.

How to navigate the benefits and dangers of mindfulness and other meditations is something that every culture and community must work out for itself. It’s yet another aspect of how Buddhism needs to be continually translated into our own time and place and adapted to harmonize with our own needs and cultural expectations.

In the West, many meditation teachers and researchers alike are now calling for informed consent , better screening and training for teachers and clinicians to recognize when practice has the potential to become dangerous. Some experts feel that therapeutic meditation should carry a warning label , like any other medical intervention that is both a potential cure and a potential risk.

Western promoters, practitioners, app developers and scholars of meditation alike have long ignored, dismissed or been completely unaware of the potential downsides. But the inconvenient fact that meditation is not always beneficial has long been familiar to the Buddhist tradition, which has a lot to say on this topic that may prove helpful.
Pierce Salguero has received funding for this research from the Institute of East-West Medicine and the Robert H.N. Ho Family Foundation.

articles.title: Why an overactive immune system attacks the bodies of people with lupus but still leaves them vulnerable to infection
articles.author:
<name>Andrew Monteith, Assistant Professor of Microbiology, University of Tennessee</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/andrew-monteith-2367958"/>
paras: Despite having an overactive immune system, people with lupus may still struggle to fight bacterial infections. My team and I found that this paradox may be because chronic inflammation pushes their immune cells toward the wrong kind of response.

To understand why an overactive immune system can still fail to control bacterial infection, we focused on neutrophils , which are white blood cells that are among the first to respond when bacteria enter the body. Neutrophils can release webs of DNA and antimicrobial proteins called neutrophil extracellular traps, or NETs , that can trap bacteria, limiting their spread and killing them.
Scientists often discuss these traps as if they are all the same, but the body can produce NETs through different pathways , and they do not all work equally well.

For example, healthy neutrophils responding to infection from Staphylococcus aureus can sense lactate, a chemical byproduct made by the bacteria. That signal helps trigger neutrophils to release a type of NET that serves as a trap rich in antibacterial proteins, but also kills the neutrophil.

In lupus, my team and I found that inflammatory molecules interfere with this antibacterial response in mice. These signals reduced levels of a protein needed to sense bacterial lactate. At the same time, another inflammatory molecule pushed neutrophils toward another form of NET it could release more quickly, sparing the neutrophil but less effective at killing bacteria.
The result is not an immune system that is weak, but an immune response that is highly active but misdirected.

Lupus is usually described as an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body’s own tissues. But serious infections are also a major concern for people with lupus. Some of that risk comes from medications that suppress the immune system, but the disease itself can also alter how immune cells function.
Our findings help explain why more inflammation does not necessarily mean better protection from infection. The type and timing of the immune response matter.

We also found that treatments currently used for lupus can correct specific defects in these neutrophil pathways. Our results do not show that people taking standard lupus treatments will have fewer infections, but they do suggest that existing therapies can correct immune defects that may contribute to susceptibility to infection.

The immune system is more complicated than one cell type or one response. Although we found that standard lupus treatments reduced the number of bacteria in several organs in lupus-prone mice, they did not significantly improve survival compared with untreated mice. Other immune cells, tissue damage and additional features of lupus likely contribute to poor outcomes during infection.

There is also an ongoing debate about what neutrophil extracellular traps actually do in lupus. Some studies have found that disrupting pathways required for NETs to form does not necessarily improve lupus, challenging the idea that simply making more NETs drives the disease.

Our findings suggest that what kind of NET neutrophils make and under what circumstances may be more important questions for lupus. During infection, lupus neutrophils may produce a type of NET that is less effective at killing bacteria while still releasing inflammatory material. That combination of poor infection control together with an inappropriate inflammatory response might exacerbate lupus.

My team and I are now focused on understanding how different types of NETs affect autoimmune disease and infection. Rather than treating all NETs as the same response, we want to define how different NETs are generated, what they contain and whether particular kinds are protective or harmful in different contexts.
Understanding how lupus changes the type of NET response produced during infection may help explain why disease activity, infection risk and treatment response vary among patients.
The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work.
Andrew Monteith receives funding from National Institute of General Medical Sciences, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, and Pew Charitable Trust.

articles.title: How the American revolt against Flock cameras mirrors the Boston Tea Party of 1773
articles.author:
<name>G. Patrick O'Brien, Assistant Professor of History, University of Tampa</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/g-patrick-obrien-694433"/>
paras: A grassroots revolt against automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, has gained momentum across the United States .
ALPRs are AI-powered cameras that capture images of all passing vehicles . The camera systems turn details into datapoints searchable by anyone with access to the information.

Today, there are more than 130,000 ALPRs on U.S. streets . And more than 5,000 law enforcement agencies use cameras produced by a single manufacturer, Flock Safety , which says its cameras have helped law enforcement agencies identify and arrest criminals and reduce crime .

But some members of those police departments have abused the data gathered by ALPRs . A police officer in Kansas was sentenced to 18 months probabtion in April 2023 for using Flock camera to stalk his estranged wife. A Florida police officer was fired and arrested in March 2026 for using data gathered by ALPRs to stalk a woman he had previously harassed on a TV set . And activists filed a lawsuit against California police departments in October 2021 for illegally sharing information collected from ALPRs with out-of-state and federal agencies, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Due to public outcry, cities across the U.S. have rejected and canceled contracts with Flock. In September 2026, Florida’s Department of Transportation revoked permits for ALPRs on its highway system.

That has not been enough to quell growing backlash over the cameras. In at least 36 states, opponents of the technology have taken matters into their own hands, destroying or impairing ALPRs rather than wait for local governments to step in.
As a historian of the American Revolution , I see parallels between Americans’ revolt against ALPRs and colonists’ destructive and often violent pushback to late 18th-century British rule.

If this summer’s celebrations marking the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding failed to inspire widespread patriotism , the increasingly bipartisan revolution against ALPRs suggests Americans have not entirely lost their rebellious spirit.

From the start, the English colonists of North America proved to be a thorn in the side of the government. Despite British hopes that investing in American colonies would enrich England , these ventures proved to be more costly than they were profitable. Colonists bore much of the blame.
When the British Parliament passed laws meant to regulate trade in the 1660s , colonists across the Eastern Seaboard turned to smuggling rather than comply .

American merchants and consumers preferred to trade directly with both their fellow English colonists and merchants in the French and Dutch colonies rather than have that trade controlled by ministers in London.
The British government had little ability to enforce the law.

That changed in 1763, after British forces vanquished the French Empire from North America at tremendous cost . A new prime minister, George Grenville, led a series of reforms aimed at making the colonists pay for their own military protection .
Many Americans often believe that the Revolution began as a revolt against higher taxes. But most of the reforms coming from London actually lowered taxes to make smuggled goods less appealing.
What colonists really resented was the imperial government’s growing influence in their lives .

In 1767, Parliament passed a series of laws that allowed Britain to raise revenue to pay the salaries of colonial governors, attorneys general and judges. At the same time, Parliament sent troops to cities such as Boston to protect its officials. Competition for work and strained community relationships often led to violence between British soldiers and colonists .

The same year, angry colonists in Boston, New York and Philadelphia began boycotting British goods . Prominent Americans, including Benjamin Franklin and John Dickinson , endorsed these nonviolent protests.
But more radical leaders believed colonists needed to take more decisive action.
On the night of Dec. 16, 1773, members of the paramilitary group the Sons of Liberty dumped nearly £10,000 – almost US$2 million in today’s dollars – worth of privately owned tea into Boston Harbor .

A few weeks later, the Sons of Liberty struck again. This time they attacked fellow colonist and British supporter John Malcolm , covering him in tar and feathers. For five hours, they beat him and paraded him through the streets. Similar instances of destruction and violence occurred across the colonies.

The British responded harshly. In May 1774, Gen. Thomas Gage arrived at Boston as the colony’s new military governor. He implemented the so-called “ Coercive Acts ,” which closed the port of Boston and disbanded local government, among other measures.
By early 1775, Boston was besieged. Around 5,000 British troops roamed the streets, directed by Gage to gather information on the Sons of Liberty and arrest leading dissidents .

Gage hoped heightened surveillance would quell unrest. But it only pushed more citizens into the radicals’ camp. On the night of April 18, 1775, a discrete network of watchmen eluded British surveillance and famously hanged two lanterns from the steeple atop Christ Church. These beacons signaled that Gage’s troops were crossing the Charles River , on their way to seize colonial stores of gunpowder and ammunition, setting in motion the events that would begin the American Revolution.

In response to the widespread pushback to ALPRs, Flock Safety CEO Garett Langley appealed to history. In June 2026 he authored a post on the company’s website , arguing that detractors misunderstand Ben Franklin’s famous 1755 quote , “Those who would give up essential liberty to purchase a little temporary safety deserve neither liberty nor safety.”

In an August 2026 interview , Langley referenced the auto industry, noting that rather than ban cars after an uptick in collision fatalities, legislatures mandated seat belts and airbags. Drawing parallels to the contemporary debate around ALPRs, Langley suggested Americans should again prioritize safety and hoped Americans would be willing to “compromise” on issues of privacy.

Samuel Adams, one of the most prominent leaders of the Sons of Liberty, had his own opinion on compromise. Writing in June 1771 , he explained that although Americans had “disagreed among themselves in one mode of opposition to arbitrary measures,” they were “united in the main principles of constitutional & natural liberty.”
Adams believed that, when threatened, American colonists would come together to defend their liberties. Clearly, Adams’ opinion resonates today.

articles.title: Helion funding round grows to $500M amid uncertainty over fusion startup’s Microsoft timeline
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Helion Energy on Tuesday said that it added $35 million to a funding round initially announced in June. The Everett, Wash.-based fusion company originally shared news of a $465 million Series G round.

“After initially closing the round earlier this summer, we are excited to bring on several new investors and to have a round that includes crossover, pension, and sovereign wealth investors,” said David Kirtley, Helion’s co-founder and CEO, in a post on LinkedIn . Kirtley said the investment now totals $500 million.

The company aims to be the first in the world to commercialize fusion, replicating the reactions that power the sun and stars to produce nearly limitless clean energy. It has raised more than $1.5 billion to date.
Last week Helion celebrated the opening of its first office in downtown Seattle as its headcount tops 800 employees.

The company is racing to hit an ambitious timeline, having signed a deal with Microsoft three years ago to supply energy to a Central Washington data center by 2028. The company broke ground on the 50-megawatt plant, dubbed Orion, in July 2025.

But Helion’s timing for hitting that energy target remains uncertain. When it announced the agreement with Microsoft, the company stated that Orion was “expected to be online by 2028 and will target power generation of 50 MW or greater after a 1-year ramp up period.”

Axios recently reported that full capacity might not be hit until 2030, according to a Helion executive. The news site also cited two scientific publications by plasma physicists questioning the company’s ability to produce a sufficient amount of energy from its fusion devices to power the grid, though Helion has responded to concerns raised by both on its FAQ site .

That said, Helion is hustling to resolve technical challenges. GeekWire in May reported on Tiny Merge , a small-scale testbed device the company is building at its R&D facility to answer questions its larger, more expensive prototypes haven’t — questions that need answers before final power plant designs are locked in.
Kirtley, however, remains bullish on the company’s trajectory and the vote of support from investors.

“Technical milestones remain the most important to me and the company,” he said, “but this new funding demonstrates the growing demand for, and confidence in, fusion energy and Helion’s ability to deliver fusion energy to the grid.”

articles.title: Terry Myerson retires as Truveta CEO, with co-founders stepping in to lead $1B health data startup
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Terry Myerson , the former Microsoft executive who co-founded Truveta during the pandemic, growing it to 500 employees and a valuation of more than $1 billion, is retiring as CEO of the Bellevue, Wash.-based health data company at the end of September.

Truveta co-founders Jay Nanduri , CTO, and Ryan Ahern , the chief medical officer, will take over as interim co-CEOs while the board conducts a search for a permanent CEO. Myerson said in an interview that the board has a responsibility to look for “the absolute best CEO,” but he expressed hope that the search will confirm Nanduri and Ahern as the right leaders for Truveta’s next chapter.

Myerson, 54, will become an advisor to the company and step down from its board. He said he’s leaving because the business is doing well and his co-founders are ready. He also cited changes in his personal life. He and his wife, Katie, are empty nesters, and they want to travel.
“If things were not going well, I would not do this,” he said. “I’d be grinding it out. But things are going really well.”

Truveta pools de-identified patient records from 30 large U.S. health systems into a database that’s updated daily. It sells access to that data, along with analysis and AI tools, to drug makers, medical device companies, researchers and government agencies studying how treatments work in the real world.

In a LinkedIn post announcing his retirement, Myerson noted that Truveta started “with an idea and no employees, no technology, no customers, and no data.” He wrote that what he’ll remember most are “the hundreds of Truvetans who took a chance on an ambitious idea and turned it into something real.”

Origins in the pandemic: Truveta grew out of a proposal from Providence, the Seattle-area nonprofit health system, for health systems to pool their data for research. Early in the pandemic, then-Providence CEO Rod Hochman called Myerson, who had left Microsoft in 2018 after leading its Windows and Devices Group, and asked him to build it.
GeekWire first reported on the startup in October 2020, and it launched publicly in February 2021 with 14 health systems.

Ahern was treating patients at NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center in New York at the time. “We were giving out hydroxychloroquine, not knowing that it was actually harming patients,” he said. “It was the first time in my career that we were learning a new disease from scratch.”

Ahern was connected to Myerson through Madrona co-founder Jerry Grinstein , a former Delta Air Lines CEO and Ahern’s uncle by marriage. Myerson had joined the Seattle venture firm as a venture partner after leaving Microsoft.

Truveta says its data now covers more than 140 million patients. It published the first peer-reviewed real-world comparison of Ozempic and Mounjaro for weight loss, research that landed the company on the Today Show .

In 2025, Truveta raised $320 million in a round that included Regeneron and Illumina, bringing its total funding to $515 million. The round helped fund the Truveta Genome Project , which is sequencing leftover blood samples from consenting patients and linking the genetic data to de-identified medical records.

State of the business: Myerson declined to share revenue figures. He acknowledged that Truveta isn’t yet profitable but said it doesn’t need to raise more money. An IPO isn’t on the near-term horizon, he said, because Truveta’s revenue isn’t yet large enough for the public markets.
That leaves Nanduri, Ahern and the board with strategic decisions about which path to take over the long term. Myerson said the company has turned down offers, without elaborating.
“One of the problems with a business that’s doing well is you’ve got all those options,” he said.
“We’re blessed with a lot of options,” Ahern added.

Dividing the job: Nanduri, a former Microsoft technical fellow, will continue to lead engineering, product and the data systems behind them. Ahern, a physician who remains on the University of Washington faculty part time, will run sales, marketing, customer delivery and the evidence services team that handles regulatory work for customers.
Nanduri described it as supply and demand. “Ryan takes care of demand,” he said. “I make sure that the supply and the ecosystem and everything thrives.”

The company is expanding beyond data into AI tools for research, including Truveta Intelligence, which launched in April and lets researchers ask questions of its clinical data in plain English. Ahern said a key challenge is showing that AI-generated answers can be trusted for high-stakes decisions such as drug safety and label expansion.

Nanduri said each of the companies behind the leading AI models is doing some health-related work, and “they have approached us too.” The board has discussed how Truveta can coexist with them, he said. The company also opened a development center in Hyderabad, India, in July, expanding its engineering organization.

Truveta’s next chapter: The leadership change follows a shift at the board level. In March, Henry Ford Health executive Robin Damschroder succeeded Hochman as Truveta’s board chair after he retired from Providence and affiliated entities.
The company also added a new senior executive this year, hiring Johnathan Lancaster , an oncologist and former Regeneron executive, as president and chief scientific officer in January.

Asked whether the board changes played a role in his decision, Myerson praised both Hochman and Damschroder, describing her as a disciplined board chair, and said the transitions are all part of the company moving into its second chapter. When it comes to CEO succession, he said, the question is who will commit for the next five to seven years.
“It’s easier for me to say, gosh, Jay and Ryan have earned this,” he said. “Bet on them for the next five to seven years versus betting on me.”
Myerson’s competitive streak, well known from his Microsoft days, hasn’t faded.

Truveta is currently No. 3 on the GeekWire 200 , our list of the top Pacific Northwest startups. Even as he discussed his departure, Myerson made his case for the top spot, calling Truveta “an amazing Pacific Northwest success story” and noting that more than 200 of its 500 employees are in the Seattle area.

At this stage of his life, he didn’t rule out the possibility of a next professional chapter for himself. But asked about his immediate plans, he said he’s hoping for “a great ski year.”

articles.title: RIP Bok a Bok — The ‘Bokin’ adventure’ is over
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Capitol Hill food and drink is up to its elbows in chicken these days but we’re still going to miss Bok a Bok . After a nine-year run next to Neumos , the Hill’s original Korean fried chicken joint has closed permanently.

The shutdown comes after a long closure for critical emergency repairs and structural damage in the floors directly beneath the cook line inside the more than 110-year-old Pike/Pine auto row-era building in a space that has suffered through the pipeline pains of deep frying for at least twenty years.

“Damage was substantial and lots has happened with our lives since the floor debacle so we are not going to be able to continue our Bokin` adventure,” owner Brian O’Connor said in an update to friends shared on social media .

CHS talked with O’Connor about the extensive and expensive construction job in January as he was hoping to get the busy counter spot back in motion. The Bok a Bok work also meant a few weeks of downtime for the Neumos underground sibling Barboza .
I turns out, Bok a Bok Capitol Hill’s final crispy chicken was served last October. RIP.

O’Connor opened the first location in White Center and expanded with new locations but the 10th Ave restaurant sandwiched next to Neumos at the corner of 10th and Pike had become the only remaining Bok a Bok in the city.

Its Capitol Hill space was previously home to the much-hyped but underwhelming arrival of the Paseo chain on Capitol Hill. Before that, it was home to Pike Street Fish Fry before it closed in 2015 after a near eight-year run.
Anything that might come next will face some expensive infrastructure repairs.

As for chicken, the neighborhood flock of choices has grown exponentially. The latest Pike/Pine poultry addition will come on 11th Ave where influencer chef Matt Broussard and the Bellevue-based Conscious Hospitality Group are teaming up to open Char the Chicken , a “fire-grilled rotisserie chicken” concept replacing, yes, sustainable chicken sandwich joint Mt. Joy . Bock a bock, indeed.

articles.title: Char the Chicken: Influencer chef and restaurant group ready to hatch new grill concept on Capitol Hill
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A growing Pacific Northwest incubator of restaurant chain concepts emphasizing health and sustainability is being joined by a celebrity chef for a high-profile poultry re-start on Capitol Hill.

The Conscious Hospitality Group is preparing the 11th Ave space formerly home to the flagship location of scuttled sustainable chicken sandwich concept Mt. Joy for a reboot as Char the Chicken , a “fire-grilled rotisserie chicken” concept that Instagram-famous Matt Broussard told the Seattle Times will overcome the challenging realities of the current Seattle dining economy because of his passion.
“Any other social media cook, they’re not gonna open a restaurant,” Broussard tells the Times. “Like, this is the dumbest thing you could do.”
The Conscious Hospitality Group backing will help.

CHG is a Bellevue-based restaurant collective and incubator led by co-founders Norman Wu and Danny Brawer . The company dedicated to “health, sustainability, and ethical business practices” pairs in-house concept development with operating partnerships, providing shared infrastructure, supply-chain scale, and administrative backing needed to expand sustainable, wellness-oriented food brands across the Pacific Northwest.

Privately held and so far free of institutional venture capital, CHG operates on an operator-funded growth-equity model. The company says it reinvests operating cash flows and savings from operational efficiencies from its high-volume, more mature concepts to self-fund earlier-stage ventures. The structure leverages buying power for things like certified sustainable proteins and 100% compostable packaging, while also reducing expansion risk as it tests new concepts.

CHG’s portfolio hits all the hours of the day, Its core expansion engine so far has been Just Poké while companion concepts like Sugo Hand Roll Bar and Hap’s Burgers adapt counter-service efficiency into urban sushi and comfort food. Complementing these are morning-to-midday wellness concepts like Sano Café and Matcha Magic , alongside low-overhead food hall testbeds like KODE Pizza, Club Seltzer, and EatDirt , which share prep logistics and validate experimental concepts before wider launches.

This framework played out on 11th Ave in March as the street’s Mt. Joy Chicken sandwich outlet suddenly shuttered ending long-term plans for aggressive expansion after a three-year run. Mt. Joy started with tech investor Robbie Cape’s plans to team up with prolific Capitol Hill and Seattle-wide restaurateur Ethan Stowell to launch Mt. Joy at 11th and Pine with the first of what they said they said would hatch into a 1,000 or more location chain focused solely on “pasture-raised” chicken. But early this year, CHG quietly pulled the plug.

Now with CHG executives on the paperwork, Broussard is the face of a new concept hoped to restore the 11th and Pine spot’s place in the restaurant group’s growing framework. The block is also home to another CHG brand, Matcha Magic, while the corner of 11th and Pine features the neighborhood’s location of Sweetgreen along with the salad chain’s “salad chutes” and “infinite kitchen” technology. Above rises the 2014-era preservation incentive-boosted Sunset Electric apartment building. The corner was famously at the center of the 2020 CHOP protests.

Broussard, known online as @acooknamedmatt , is a Texas-born, Seattle-based chef, cookbook author of Now We’re Cooking , and prominent food creator. After training at Le Cordon Bleu in Austin and working his way up through the Tom Douglas empire in Seattle, he gained a massive digital following during the pandemic with his energetic, ASMR-style videos and rapid knife work.
In media interviews earlier this year, Broussard said the new rotisserie chicken venture was hoped for a summer launch in time for Seattle’s host games during the FIFA World Cup .
Broussard tells the Times the Capitol Hill start of the Char the Chicken concept is now planned to launch in October.
Char the Chicken is opening at 1531 11th Ave. Follow @charthechicken for updates.

articles.title: Wilson slows homelessness plan including shelter goals in roll-out of 2027 budget proposal
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Belmont Village opened on Capitol Hill this summer

Mayor Katie Wilson is adjusting her homelessness plan , stretching out the timeline, funding mechanisms, and scope to bring more unhoused people indoors while managing an inherited $175 million budget deficit.

Saying her updated plan “doesn’t promise quick fixes that paper over real problems,” Wilson said this week the changes are part of her proposed budget that will be released next Tuesday, the first budget under the Wilson administration.

While Wilson’s core goals remain in place including the establishment of approximately 1,000 emergency shelter spaces paired with wraparound services, budget realities are going to slow things down. In March, the administration framed the delivery of 1,000 shelter units as a single-year objective for 2026. The September update extends that goal through the end of 2027, scheduling 960 total beds to serve an estimated 1,750 people annually across facilities established in 2026 and eight sites slated for 2027.

Fiscal and operational costs have also grown. The updated plan directs $37 million toward shelter capacity and allocates $11.2 million in 2027 toward rental assistance, eviction prevention, and legal aid. The approach places greater emphasis on acute care, citing King County survey data showing 33% of unhoused individuals experience substance use disorders and 27% report serious mental illness. The plan also incorporates the return of homelessness contracting to the city from the King County Regional Homelessness Authority .
Addressing the deficit challenges, Wilson said her updated homelessness plan will rely on existing revenues redirected within the upcoming 2027–2028 budget.

Despite an executive order in the early weeks of her administration and the launch of a new Tiny House Village-focused strategy this spring, Wilson has made only slow progress on increasing the city’s shelter capacity. While Belmont Village opened with 31 new shelter homes on Capitol Hill in July , Wilson’s acceleration plan has produced only 75 additional new units at a new village in Interbay.

articles.title: Bellevue Council Faces Decision Point on Parking Reform
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Eastside's largest city is grappling with a new state mandate to scale back its off-street parking requirements for new development. In facing choices around going further than the new state-required baseline, Bellevue's leaders are facing crosswinds: a desire to continue reducing barriers to homebuilding is crashing into the city's car-oriented status quo.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

The new mandate is coming thanks to Senate Bill 5184 , a law approved last year that sets strict caps on the number of off-street parking stalls that Washington cities can require with new building projects. By next January, Bellevue will no longer be able to require more than one parking stall for every two apartment units, nor more than two parking stalls for every 1,000 square feet of commercial space.

The City will also be barred from requiring any parking for a broad set of uses, including apartments less than 1,200 square feet in size, commercial spaces that are less than 3,000 square feet, child care facilities, and affordable and senior housing.

The statewide parking reform is intended to ease cost burdens on builders, which are passed along to renters and homebuyers. Adding garage parking typically costs builders $60,000 per stall or more, according to the housing-focused Pacific Northwest think tank Sightline Institute.

Cities across the state are grappling with the new requirements, but Bellevue's size, prevalence of transit infrastructure, and positive trends in housing permit starts are putting a spotlight on how this new mandate gets implemented. Earlier this year, numerous councilmembers expressed clear interest in looking at how to be more ambitious in giving developers flexibility around parking, but recommendations that came out of Bellevue's planning commission hew much closer to the bare minimum.

A growing number of Washington cities are taking steps to fully eliminate parking mandates from their land use codes, following in the footsteps of places like Spokane , Port Townsend , and Bellingham . Vancouver abolished parking mandates as part of its Comprehensive Plan update earlier this year, with Tacoma next on deck. Next door to Bellevue in Issaquah, city leaders are considering eliminating mandates across a wide swath of the center city – an area where increasing housing growth is the goal.

A full repeal is likely a step too far for Bellevue, no matter the studies showing the range of positive benefits that come from doing so. Earlier this year, UCLA's Institute of Transportation Studies published a new research synthesis looking at a range of studies considering the impact of arbitrary requirements to build parking and the quantified benefits that come from wiping them off the books.

"Across the research literature, scholars generally recommend eliminating minimum parking requirements. Removing these mandates lifts a major barrier to new housing and businesses, reduces the risk of parking oversupply, and encourages more efficient use of existing spaces," the researchers noted. "Slowing the growth of parking infrastructure can improve walkability and urban design, reduce environmental harms, and support more sustainable travel behavior."
A full repeal is likely a step too far for Bellevue officials, so instead the debate will focus on pulling a few additional levers.

"Considering that we have appropriately aggressive housing goals, and that many projects are struggling to move forward, I think we should continue to keep our foot on the gas. And I think there are some modifications we should consider to the final code, so that we can do that," Bellevue Deputy Mayor Dave Hamilton said last week.

By 2029, Bellevue will need to remove parking mandates from within a half-mile walk of light rail stations and within a quarter-mile of RapidRide bus stops. The city is going ahead and making that update now, but the council could expand that radius to a half-mile distance from RapidRide stations, which includes the B Line and the K Line , planned to open by 2030.

"Council has already established policy direction that we want more housing capacity near high-capacity transit, including allowing six units by right in a half mile of light rail and quarter mile of bus rapid transit [BRT], removing mandatory parking requirements in those areas that are transit served is consistent with the broader direction," Councilmember Vishal Bhargava said. "I would ask that we consider [...] the half mile around the BRT, and just as an analysis to see what the puts and takes would be towards that."
Naren Briar was the only councilmember to bring up the idea of a full repeal of parking mandates, laying down a potential marker for the future.

"I am personally interested in exploring citywide elimination of parking minimums. According to the research I did, cities like Austin, San Jose, Buffalo, had done this and seen a tremendous amount of economic boost as a result of that. So I do want us to, to be clear, I think if we did that now, it might cause a little bit of chaos," Briar said. "But I do want us eventually to see a city that is comprehensively integrated and allows end-to-end walkability as an effective mode of transportation for senior citizens, for young kids waiting at the bus stop, for for any resident or visitor of Bellevue."

Another issue likely to come up before a final vote in October is visitor parking. The draft code approved by the planning commission includes a set of requirements on top of the minimum required parking stalls for residential units, mandating every development with more than six units include one visitor stall for every 20 units. After 50 units or 20,000 square feet of gross floor area that requirement no longer applies, bizarrely.

"I'm inclined to think that our mandate should be eliminated, and I'm looking to Seattle and Redmond, where they don't have any visitor parking mandate," Hamilton said. "I think housing providers understand their customers' preferences and will build projects accordingly. This may be an area where we can follow the lead of neighboring cities and help ensure that folks who move here are not penalized."

There will also be a push in the other direction. At last Tuesday's meeting, a clear bloc formed in favor of sticking with the planning commission recommendation that included Jared Nieuwenhuis, Lynne Robinson, and Claire Sumadiwirya.

"Myself, I live in a townhouse community, so I would say if there's no visitor parking, somebody is not able to walk a half mile, take the light rail, then nobody's gonna ever visit me," Sumadiwirya said. "I have a lot of elderly friends, so I think it's really important to know that. I appreciate the take of meet the state minimum first. I think whenever there's something [that] changes in the policy, it's always good to be safe and finding that balance versus just I think making drastic, too bold changes that will be different."

Robinson, who served as Bellevue's mayor from 2020 to 2025, went even further than her colleagues and suggested that the city might make a push to amend state law to mandate parking at senior living facilities. She pushed back most strenuously on the idea of going further than the planning commission recommendation.

"Nobody's going to have service providers serve the seniors. Nobody's going to get a visitor, and Silver Glen is our only, I think, our only independent [living facility]," Robinson said. "I guess there's one next to Emerald Court, but independent senior living, and all those people have cars, and most of them cannot walk that far, so they're staying connected to the community by having the ability to drive, and if we take the parking away, it's going to really limit people's ability to live independently."

According to the National Resources Defense Council , 37.6% of Americans over the age of 75 have driving limitations, as of 2025. Nothing in the land use code would limit the ability for developers of senior and independent living facilities from building off-street parking with their projects – removing the mandate simply gets the city out of the business of deciding what's appropriate.
While not likely to represent a major sea change, the October 20 vote on parking reform will certainly signal what direction Bellevue is heading.

articles.title: Suite Deal
articles.author: Harry Cheadle
paras: All summer long, if you walked around Seattle’s Stadium District during the day you probably heard the sounds of the labor movement at work—chants and exclamations from the striking unionized employees at Hilton’s Embassy Suites hotel picketing their employer for better wages and working conditions.

Things are quieter now. After an 85-day work stoppage, workers signed a contract last Thursday night that union officials say amounts to a “tremendous win,” according to a press release. They went on strike June 18 and the work stoppage lasted nearly three months including during the height of the FIFA World Cup, making it the longest hotel strike in Washington state history, according to UNITE HERE Local 8, the union representing the workers.

One of the most groundbreaking aspects of the new contract, is year-round health insurance for employees who have worked at least 1,250 hours the prior year (an average of 24 hours a week), according to Jus Adsuara, a member of the housekeeping staff and a union shop steward.That’s a rare benefit among even unionized hotels, Adsuara says.Previously, workers who got assigned fewer shifts after the peak summer months could temporarily lose their insurance as their hours dipped.

The union earned wins on wages, too: Next year starting pay for Embassy Suites housekeepers will rise to $31 per hour, a 6.9 percent raise, while tipped workers will see a $1 per hour bump on top of Seattle’s minimum wage of $21.30. In response to demands that Hilton increase staffing levels , housekeepers will have their workload reduced, and front desk workers can now file grievances if they are overworked.

The union also scored concessions on immigration-related issues, a sticking point for the workforce, which the union says is mostly immigrants. Employees wanted supervisors to alert staff whenever Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) or other Department of Homeland personnel were at the hotel—a legitimate concern given that the World Cup brought additional officers to Seattle and signs of increased ICE presence all over Washington state. There is now a labor-management committee that can address emergency situations when ICE shows up at the hotel. Additionally, employees who lose their jobs because their work authorizations expire can return to their jobs within two years.

The union won these concessions after a few months where the union and management barely communicated, says Adsuara. “Apart from a really uneventful [bargaining] session on day 12 of the strike, we had over 70 days of no contact from the company,” the strike leader says. “It was this huge battle of attrition and confidence between both sides of the bargaining table, waiting for the other to give.”

The union didn’t cave. A strike fund helped workers defray the costs of not working, but it didn’t replace all of their lost wages, according to Adsuara. While they were out picketing, Embassy Suites workers were supported by local politicians, including Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, who both walked the picket line on Labor Day. Representatives from other local unions also joined the picket line .

“This agreement reflects a collaborative outcome and our commitment to our valued Team Members,” Hilton said in a statement to the Stranger . “We look forward to welcoming our Team Members back to work and continuing to deliver exceptional hospitality to our guests.”

The immediate reaction to the contract agreement on Thursday was “a big sigh of relief” from workers, says Adsuara. The day started at 6 a.m. on the picket line and the final bargaining session stretched late into the evening. But getting over the finish line was worth it. “I’m feeling pretty proud,” they say.

paras: Dear Readers: I’m on vacation — second and last week — and will be back with new columns next week. Please enjoy this selection of letters from three previously published columns in the meantime. — Dan

I was told by the church to save it for marriage and I was a virgin until met the woman who would become my wife at a party. What do I do? How do I tell her? And is there any way I can come out of this a good husband?

I was so relieved to get all the way to end of your letter without learning you had kids. Because that means I can advise you — with a clear conscience — to file for divorce and move the fuck out just as soon as it’s possible to do so. Not for your own sake, ITS, but for your wife’s sake. She deserves better.

You say you’re growing increasingly resentful. I hope your resentment is directed at all of the people who victimized you. Your wife isn’t one of them. It’s your parents you should resent, ITS, as well as all the sex-phobic bullshit artists out there masquerading as “faith leaders.”

You should be angry with yourself. While I know from personal experience how a religious upbringing can put the zap on a kid’s head, you were a grown-ass man when you met your wife at that party. You couldn’t have slept with her that night — you couldn’t have lost your virginity in a one-night stand — if you hadn’t already rejected nearly everything you’d been taught about sex. And if you were capable of having premarital sex, ITS, you were capable of refraining from marrying the first person you slept with.

Your wife is gonna want to know why you’re leaving her — because of course she is — but you’re not going to tell her the real reason. You’re going to make something up. You want kids and she doesn’t (or vice-versa), you married too young (which is true), you have unresolved childhood issues (and don’t we all). You can’t be a good husband to her, ITS, but you can be decent ex-husband. And to do that — to be her decent and loving and supportive ex — you can’t set her self-esteem on fire on your way out the door.

And your wife’s body isn’t repulsive. She’s not someone you’re attracted to, ITS, and you’re not obligated to find short and round women sexually appealing. But while “tall and slim” are more closely associated with conventional concepts of attractiveness, ITS, not everyone’s into tall and slim. There are people out there who are into short and round and people who who are attracted to all body types and people who are indifferent to bodies. Your wife deserves the chance to be with someone who’s sincerely attracted to her. Even being alone would be better than spending decades with someone who recoils from her touch.

And for the record: What’s on the inside does count. It matters. If you met a woman who was more conventionally attractive — if you were with someone who was your idea of hot — and over time she revealed herself to be an asshole (signs: rude to waiters, shitty about your friends, a Trump supporter, etc.), your attraction to her would wither away. What you want — the best you can hope for — is some combo of hot on the outside (subjective and personal) and good on the inside. And the longer you’re with someone, ITS, the more important that good on the inside shit becomes. Time is a meat grinder that makes hamburger us all. If you prioritize your idea of hot over all other qualities, you run the very real risk of spending decades with a person who has aged out of hot and was never nice.

Married 40-year-old gay guy here. I hate beards—the look, the feel, the smell — and I miss the good old days when the only beards gay dudes had were metaphorical. I agree that it’s his body and his choice, but I think he should still take me into consideration, and that it’s actually him who’s rejecting me, by choosing the beard over me. What’s your take?
Spouse’s Hairiness Averts Virile Erection

I’m on your side, SHAVE, but I’m also on his. It is his body, and growing a beard is something he can choose to do with the face section of his body. But that my body/my choice stuff cuts both ways: Your body is yours , and what you do with your body is your choice. paras: Your uncle is wrong about crime in downtown Seattle: Crime is down citywide in 2026 compared to 2018, contrary to the popular television news narrative. The neighborhood with the lowest crime rate is downtown. Why did places ike South Lake Union (SLU) get more dangerous than downtown? articles.title: Mayor Katie Wilson Presents Gun Violence Prevention Plan
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson is rolling out a plan to tackle gun violence by better integrating city departments and maintaining services for youth. The announcement comes after weeks of relentless criticism of the city’s public safety track record by local corporate media and a slew of big businesses following the Bite of Seattle mass shooting in July.

Flanked by Seattle Police Department (SPD) Interim Chief Andre Sayles and CARE Department Chief Amy Barden, Wilson sat down with The Stranger and explained that the city had to do more to break down silos between the two public safety agencies.

As part of the plan, the CARE Department , which operates Seattle’s 911 call center and a team of 40 non-police crisis responders, is being given a bigger role. Wilson’s budget proposal will keep the department’s gun violence director and fund an additional gun violence coordinator. The department is also taking over nine contracts with nonprofits—worth about $5 million annually—to do violence interruption work for the city.
Barden says transferring the contracts will enable CARE department responders to quickly know when a young person in crisis has already been working with a case manager or mentor.

One obstacle to the CARE Department’s success has been the City’s labor contract with the Seattle Police Officers Guild (SPOG), which represents rank-and-file cops. In August, Seattle’s Office of the Inspector General released a report claiming that the CARE department’s “scope of work remains significantly impacted” by the SPOG contract, which requires all 911 calls to be routed through a dual dispatch system that includes SPD officers.

Barden rejected the idea that the SPOG contract could throw a wrench in Wilson’s gun violence plan, saying “the contracts really don’t matter as long as the first responders know how to hand off to each other.”

Barden cited internal data suggesting that over the last six weeks, the CARE Department’s responder utilization rate has gone up to 80 percent as cops are diverting more cases. Last year during the same time, the team was only utilizing about 40 percent of its capacity, CARE Department spokesperson Bobbie Nickel says.

A large part of this could be due to the department’s expansion in early August, which broadened the crisis response window to 18 hours a day and nearly doubled its force. The growth was funded by a recent 0.1 percent sales tax hike .

Sayles said that under his leadership SPD management has been pushing rank-and-file officers to divert more calls to the CARE Department and clear up misinformation about the limitations of the SPOG contract. Sayles was deputy chief at SPD for a year and has been the acting police chief for seven weeks.

“Our supervisors [are] really diving into it and making those connections, understanding that we have a lot of work that we do on a daily basis as police officers, and saying this isn’t our wheelhouse,” Sayles says.

Wilson also pledged to increase SPD foot and cyclist patrols in Belltown, Little Saigon, Rainier Beach, and along Aurora Avenue North. She said this is the first step of a “focused deterrence” approach, which is essentially a carrot and stick strategy where punishment is paired with offers of services and diversion.

On top of the CARE team capacity changes, Wilson believes youth services can help ameliorate rising gun violence. The upcoming budget conversation will be difficult—the city is facing a $175 million budget deficit. But Wilson maintained she will shield funding for youth services. That includes maintaining mental health care investments and allocating $600,000 for a new after school program in Rainier Beach, plus keeping open a ninth Teen Late Night center in West Seattle.

The City is also partnering with the University of Washington and John Hopkins University to review its gun violence prevention strategies and develop a new review process to analyze every homicide. Some city council members would like to see the City pursue different partnerships, though.

Seattle City Councilmember Martiza Rivera has introduced a resolution asking the City to adopt that model and partner with the National Network for Safer Communities. Consulting with the organization could cost the city more than $400,000 .

Embarrassingly, at a September 8 Public Safety Committee meeting discussing the resolution, Rivera mixed up Seattle’s shots fired and homicide statistics, inflating the latter count by “an order of magnitude ,” as Publicola reported. Since 2024, homicides in Seattle have been trending downward. In the first eight months of 2026, the City had five fewer homicides compared to the same period in 2025, a 23 percent decrease.

Wilson said the City was already working on a focused deterrence strategy, and that, although she shared the same goals as the council member, Rivera “has a little bit of a different idea for how to get there.”
Ultimately, Wilson says although there is no “magic solution” to gun violence, her collection of strategies could bring down the numbers further.
“We are making progress—gun violence is down—and [yet] there is no acceptable level of violence,” Wilson says.

articles.title: Rob Saka Throws Together Traffic Safety Legislation Ahead of Council Deadline
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle Council transportation committee chair Rob Saka has been rushing forward a set of bills intended to improve traffic safety outcomes on city streets, hoping to beat a legislative deadline before this fall's budget season. The package, which consists of three separate bills , purports to give the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) additional tools to implement safety upgrades, asks for recommendations around timelines to remediate city streets following fatal crashes, and sets the City up to be able to mandate side guards on vehicles used by city contractors.
However, SDOT has confirmed with The Urbanist that the department was not fully looped in on the package's development, with Saka moving things forward on a very compressed timeline.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Saka rolled out his proposal , which he is calling the Seattle SAFER (Safe Accountable Flexible Equitable Responsive) Streets Act, two days before Mayor Katie Wilson signed an executive order that deals with many of the same topics. Saka, due to his role as committee chair, had reportedly received a briefing on the contents of that executive order, but did not appear at Wilson's press event to roll it out in Beacon Hill on August 21.
The overlap between the new executive order and Saka's legislative proposal is particularly pronounced when it comes to potential regulations around side guards and other vehicle safety retrofits.

"I suppose great minds can arrive at some of the same intersections as we appear to have done and aligned on from a legislative and executive perspective, and that's a good thing," Saka said last week, at the second committee meeting held to discuss the bills. "The two efforts are complementary, but distinct. Executive action can move quickly, [and] initiate changes today. Legislation, by comparison, can establish durable requirements that survive changes in administrations, department leadership, or priorities."

When Saka made those comments, all three of the bills remained in draft form, having missed a prior deadline for introduction and referral before the Council's August recess. Holding a committee discussion, much less two, around a draft version of a bill is unusual, and during last week's meeting several issues surfaced that conveyed how rushed the process has been thus far, including the fact that modifications recommended by the City's law department had been made between the August 20 and September 8 meeting.
So what would the SAFER Streets Act actually do?

The first bill in the package adjusts the authority of the SDOT Director, giving that position explicit authority to do many things that are already under their control. That includes the authorization (not requirement) "to ensure capital project reviews are informed by safety needs identified in a Vision Zero Plan when changes to the configuration or operations of an intersection are proposed and when geography and budget allow." It would codify a requirement that the Vision Zero Plan (which appears to be the same as a Vision Zero Action Plan) be updated every three years.

It would also ask SDOT for a report, to be delivered by next June, that considers options for "improving the Department's existing response following a qualifying fatal crash." That work would build on an internal SDOT policy, adopted in May, that codifies expectations around how the department reviews fatal crashes on city right-of-way, with a two to four-week review after SDOT receives a crash report from the Seattle Police Department and a 90-day timeframe for "remediation or maintenance activities."

That internal policy also includes a twice-yearly review of all crashes involving people who were walking, rolling, biking, or using a scooter or motorcycle. That data is used to inform Vision Zero investments with a goal of making safety upgrades within two years of that review.

Saka's bill asks for at least three "progressively more stringent options" for post fatal crash review, including a requirement to evaluate what it would look like to conduct a review within 72 hours of receiving a crash report, and the potential for remediation to take place within two weeks. Presumably this report would be used to inform future legislation, but the bill ultimately doesn't make any direct changes to city policies around post-crash review.

That bill also includes a section dealing with the amount of time that the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) spends reviewing potential modifications to highway on and off-ramps within the city, requesting design feedback be returned "within a reasonable amount of time, but in no case more than 180 days." But the City of Seattle has no legal standing to require any specific timelines from another level of government, turning the section into a pretty please.

The second bill in the package addresses the city position of City Traffic Engineer, a position that has been held by Venu Nemani since 2021. Nemani also holds the title of Chief Transportation Safety Officer, after being "elevated" to that role in 2023 following the release of a "top to bottom" review of the department's Vision Zero program.

The bill would not codify that Chief Transportation Safety Officer position, but rather give the City Traffic Engineer explicit authority to do things that are already commonplace, like the ability to "review and provide recommendations to enhance the safety of roadways and transportation infrastructure." It's not clear that a lack of these specific authorities is inhibiting the department from being able to make safety interventions now, and nothing in the bill would require the City Traffic Engineer to do anything differently.

The third bill, which was only discussed conceptually at the August 20 transportation committee meeting, would request requirements for vehicles operated by city contractors to have "truck lateral protective devices," commonly referred to as truck side guards. Placed along the undercarriage of a vehicle, side guards can prevent people who are walking or rolling from being pulled under the vehicle in the event of a crash.
The bill specifically calls out Boston, which codified truck side guard requirements into city code in 2014, and asks for recommendations by May 1 of next year.

During last week's meeting, members of the council's independent central staff raised issues that came from the Department of Finance and Administrative Services (FAS), which would be tasked with implementing the bill – noting that department wasn't looped in until early September.

"We were able to speak with FAS about this bill last week. Very grateful to them for jumping in and providing their analysis," legislative analyst Ann Gorman said. "They raised a couple issues which we have flagged as policy considerations. FAS may require additional resources to develop the requested recommendations. For instance, FAS does not have mechanical engineering capacity, and FAS may not have capacity to perform and/or oversee the requested body of work by the date that is currently in the ordinance."

Wilson's executive order also directed FAS to work on side guards and other potential safety enhancements for contracted vehicles, but instead asks for a report on opportunities and impacts by next January.

"The executive order is very much in a similar subject area, but it is asking for another thing," Gorman said. "It seems reasonable to expect that after the requested report is delivered [...] the mayor's office might consider developing actual requirements about what it has heard based on the opportunity and impact analysis, but that is not what it is doing."

Other members of the transportation committee, including Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Eddie Lin, have raised concerns about the fact that SDOT has not been at the table at any of the committee meetings so far.

"I would be interested in hearing SDOT's feedback, and just want to make sure that – not that we have to adopt what they say – but I do just want to make sure that this is going to work for them as well, and if there are potential concerns or tweaking of anything, that I'd like to have the time to bring those forward for discussion," Lin said.

SDOT press secretary Ethan Bergerson confirmed via email late last week that the department was only looped in on Saka's package on August 19, the day before the first committee discussion was held. SDOT did provide feedback on the bill on September 4, Bergerson said, but no changes were incorporated by the September 8 meeting when Saka assured his colleagues that no further changes would be made. The Urbanist has not yet confirmed the substance of SDOT's feedback.

Councilmembers raised other process concerns. Because the bills aren't set to be formally introduced until September 15, two days before a final committee vote, the deadline to submit amendments was last week. That means councilmembers will have not seen a final version of the bill when being asked to submit potential changes.
"I've never seen an amendment deadline for a piece of legislation that has not formally been introduced yet. How is that possible?" Rinck, the committee's vice chair, asked staff last week.
"I can only tell you that we've been working out how to make all of the pieces fit, and this is the timeline that we've developed to achieve this vote date," was the reply from analyst Amanda Allen.

Saka defended the process to develop the package, and the fact that SDOT has not been at the table for committee discussions, stating that it is common for departments to not be directly involved in meetings on proposals that originate from the legislative branch.

"My office has been working closely with SDOT on this, especially [over] the last six weeks plus, even before that, on various higher-level aspects of this," Saka said. "They have reviewed and provided my office with extensive feedback, and my office has met directly with the department, and the executive, the mayor's office, on our complimentary efforts numerous times. And I would encourage you, Councilmember Lin, vice chair [Rinck] as well, anyone, to meet directly with the department yourselves."

A final committee vote is tentatively scheduled for this Thursday, September 17. If that vote isn't taken, the package would likely be held until the council wraps up its budget work around Thanksgiving.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Building Toward a Greener, Housing-Abundant Seattle
articles.author: Logan Schmidt
paras: There’s a reason Seattle is called the Emerald City in the Evergreen State: our trees help make Seattle the vibrant city that it is. But preserving that vision doesn’t mean we have to choose between protecting them and building the housing we need. We can – and must – do both.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

In 2007, Seattle established a goal to reach 30% tree canopy coverage by 2037. At the time, the city’s canopy stood at 18%, according to the City’s Urban Forestry Management Plan . To reach their goal, the City of Seattle Urban Forestry Coalition – consisting of an interdepartmental team of staff from Seattle Parks and Recreation, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), the Office of Sustainability and the Environment, and more – put forth a list of short and long-term actions, including improving planting and maintenance of City-managed trees, strengthening incentives and regulations to encourage tree preservation on private property, and exploring new financing mechanisms to fund City-operated urban forestry programs.

Seattle has made strong progress toward that goal: the most recent tree canopy study , using data from 2021, has Seattle at 28.1% canopy coverage, an increase of 10 percentage points in 14 years – even as the city’s population grew by nearly 150,000 people and added more than 100,000 new units of housing. As the city prepares for more growth, we have an opportunity to develop new policies and investments to close the remaining gap and meet or even exceed the City’s 30% goal.

And while we continue to care for trees and our environment, Seattle is also grappling with a serious housing shortage. Under the One Seattle Plan ’s adopted growth targets, Seattle must plan for 120,000 new housing units by 2044, or roughly 6,000 homes per year.

Since 2017, Seattle added 8,300 new homes in the Neighborhood Residential (formerly Single Family) zone, typically where detached, ADUs, and moderate middle housing products are built. In lowrise, midrise, highrise, and downtown zones, where apartments are more prevalent, 27,500 units were added. However, data shows a significant downturn in permits in 2025 and 2026, which is a concerning reality for what’s to come, considering new housing takes years to move from permit to construction to occupancy.

The slowing production of housing will only further place strain on homeowners and renters in the city. Seattle homebuyers spent 54.1% of their income on housing costs in 2024, making it one of the least affordable housing markets in the country. And nearly 50% of renter households in the region are cost burdened , meaning they're paying more than 30% of their income on rent.

So, how are we, as a city and region, responding to this pressure? Well, the answer is two-fold. The One Seattle Plan is both Seattle’s Comprehensive Plan – the 20-year vision and roadmap for the city’s growth, required under Washington’s Growth Management Act (GMA) – and the vehicle through which Seattle adopted middle housing: duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes, and other “ missing middle ” housing types mandated statewide by House Bill 1110 . In other words, the same document that guides how Seattle grows responsibly is also the one legalizing more homes in more neighborhoods.

However, the GMA doesn’t just require cities like Seattle to develop comprehensive plans and regulations to guide their growth. It requires local governments to treat housing, transportation, the environment, and more as coequal goals, not competing ones.

Despite this requirement, in public debates at City Hall, goals like more housing and the environment are seemingly – and incorrectly so – pitted against each other. Seattle’s own Urban Forestry Commission has pushed back on the notion that urban density and tree canopy cannot coexist, noting that “what we need to do is better understand how we balance one and the other, while acknowledging that both are necessary.”

Why does the conversation then so often fall into a choice between the two? And instead of asking whether we can have housing or trees, maybe it’s worth asking: what policy choices let us have both ? That starts with recognizing Seattle’s role in the broader region and building on the approaches already showing that density and canopy can grow together.

When cities enact policies that limit opportunities for new housing, that new development doesn't stop – it just moves elsewhere. And that prevents people who want to live and work in a city like Seattle from accessing homes in the transit-oriented, walkable neighborhoods Seattleites and our local government have spent years investing in. Pushing people further out into car-dependent areas results in longer commutes, more vehicle miles traveled, and more emissions. It also means more roads and parking lots replacing permeable land, sending stormwater runoff into local waterways, and further harming our salmon and orca populations .

Furthermore, building new housing in the city can make our current urban environment better. According to a recent King County study of Lake Washington , from 2000 to 2020, the population of the watershed grew by 34% while developed land area grew by less than 5% and forest cover remained steady. Rather than clearing intact forest to accommodate growth, the population grew in place by converting from lower-density to higher-density housing. This new development likely prompted stormwater upgrades, septic-to-sewer transitions, and other changes that helped improve the lake’s water quality.

Not only have we seen improvements in the lake’s water quality, but we’ve also seen new construction lead to planting and protecting trees on site at a rate 325% higher than tree removals are occurring. Since July 2023, when Seattle’s Tree Protection Ordinance went into effect, more than 14,100 trees have been planted and protected during the construction of new homes compared to roughly 4,300 trees removed.

Of those trees removed during construction, nearly 88% were a Tier 3, Tier 4, or below category. The majority of the older, larger tree loss is happening entirely outside of construction: nearly 71% of all Tier 2 tree removals are non-construction-related (Tier 2 trees include trees 24 inches or greater, tree groves, and specific tree species as provided by a Director’s Rule ).

We continue to be interested in finding more ways to preserve and add trees alongside the construction of new housing. However, if protecting Seattle’s most significant trees is the goal, the data points toward paying more attention to the far larger share of removals occurring with no new housing to show for it.

Even worse, and not accounted for in the data above, the largest net change in Seattle’s canopy coverage between 2016 and 2021 occurred in publicly owned parks (“Parks Natural Areas”). Seattle’s parks saw a 5.1% canopy loss, accounting for nearly half of the city’s overall canopy loss (111 of the 255 acres lost) across all management types (neighborhood residential, right-of-way, etc.).

The public right-of-way didn’t fare much better. Over that same period, the city lost 10 acres of canopy in the right-of-way alone – land the city already owns and controls, and the same land that makes up 27% of Seattle’s total area . This points exactly to where the opportunity is: parks and the public right-of-way represent the few places the city can take action on to impact canopy growth directly.

Everyone who cares about housing and trees needs to continue to work on creative solutions for both. Many of our members continue to do that and we look forward to hearing new ideas. In the meantime, we already have solutions we can start implementing now. If new housing isn’t the leading culprit for Seattle’s canopy loss, then we should be putting less energy into pitting homebuilding against trees amidst a regional housing shortage. Rather, it’s time to get serious about growing canopy everywhere. Seattle’s already set the target: 30% canopy by 2037. Getting there means treating tree planting like the public priority it actually is.
Here’s are strategies we can start implementing now:

None of this requires choosing between a growing city and a green one – the data backs that up, and the Complete Communities Coalition laid out the case in more detail in their fact sheet, Right Tree, Right Place: A Greener, Housing-Abundant Seattle .
